⌂
Clinical Reference

Wernicke Encephalopathy

On this page
An acute, reversible thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency that starves the periventricular gray matter of ATP — and a true emergency, because the window in which it is reversible is measured in hours to days, and the treatment is a cheap, almost harmless vitamin.
Clinical diagnosis — never wait for a level or an MRI Thiamine 500 mg IV TID × ≥5 days Full triad in only 10–20% Untreated: death in up to 20%, Korsakoff in 85% of survivors MRI misses ~1 in 2 — a normal MRI does NOT rule it out
If you remember one thing: in any patient with poor intake, rapid weight loss, protracted vomiting, alcohol use disorder, or unexplained confusion — give IV thiamine now. The ASMBS 2025 task force states it plainly: WE "is a bona fide emergency as much as a myocardial infarction or stroke," and anaphylaxis to IV thiamine is roughly 1 in 5 million. There is no version of this where withholding the vitamin is the safer choice.
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story, from vitamin to lesion

Thiamine is not a drug the brain uses; it is a cofactor the brain cannot make energy without. Once absorbed, thiamine is phosphorylated to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP, also written TDP) — and that phosphorylation step requires magnesium. TPP is then the mandatory cofactor for four enzymes, three of which sit at chokepoints in glucose metabolism:

TPP-dependent enzymeWhere it sitsWhat fails without it
Pyruvate dehydrogenaseGateway from glycolysis into the TCA cyclePyruvate cannot become acetyl-CoA. Glucose is taken up but cannot be burned — it is shunted to lactate instead.
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenaseRate-limiting step inside the TCA cycleThe cycle stalls in its middle. NADH and therefore oxidative-phosphorylation ATP output collapse.
Transketolase also needs Mg²⁺Pentose phosphate pathwayLess NADPH (so less regenerated glutathione → the cell loses its antioxidant defence) and less ribose-5-phosphate (so less nucleotide and myelin lipid synthesis).
Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenaseLeucine / isoleucine / valine catabolismBranched-chain amino acids and their ketoacids accumulate; a smaller contributor to the clinical picture.

The consequences cascade. ATP failure disables the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, so cells swell — this is the cytotoxic edema you see as restricted diffusion on DWI. Astrocytes, which are themselves ATP-starved, stop clearing glutamate through their EAAT1/EAAT2 transporters, so glutamate floods the synapse, over-drives NMDA receptors, and lets calcium pour into neurons: excitotoxic cell death. Accumulating lactate drops local pH. Finally the blood–brain barrier gives way, adding vasogenic edema and the petechial hemorrhages that Carl Wernicke described in the mammillary bodies in 1881.

This is why every therapy in this guide is either thiamine (restores TPP and restarts the whole chain) or magnesium (without which thiamine cannot be converted to TPP, so the thiamine you give does nothing). There is no second drug class. Everything else — benzodiazepines, electrolytes, nutrition — is supportive care that keeps the patient alive and safe while the vitamin does the actual work.
a factory where every assembly line runs on one specialty bolt. The raw material (glucose) keeps arriving on the loading dock, the workers show up, the power is on — but without that one bolt the lines cannot turn over. Product backs up in the yard (lactate), the lights start browning out (ATP failure), and the departments that run their machines hardest — the ones that never idle — burn out first. That is why the damage is not random: it lands on the periventricular gray matter, structures with the highest thiamine-dependent metabolic turnover in the brain. And magnesium is the wrench: you can deliver a truckload of bolts, but with no wrench, none of them get installed.
The cascade from empty vitamin store to petechial hemorrhage. Note the two Mg²⁺ dependencies — they are the reason a hypomagnesemic patient can look "thiamine-refractory."
Thiamine diphosphate (= thiamine pyrophosphate, TPP): the thiamine moiety in blue, the two added phosphates in black. Adding those phosphates is the magnesium-dependent step.
Image: Michael D. Turnbull — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Thiamine diphosphate coloured.svg
Transketolase (ribbon) with TPP bound in its active site (yellow). Erythrocyte transketolase activity was the classic functional assay for thiamine status — and its magnesium requirement is why hypomagnesemia mimics thiamine deficiency.
Image: Thomas Shafee — CC BY 4.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Transketolase + TPP 2.svg
The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex — an 11-megadalton machine whose E1 subunit will not turn over without TPP. This is the single enzyme that stands between glycolysis and the TCA cycle.
Image: National Institutes of Health (NIH) — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · 3D pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.jpg
The TCA cycle. TPP is required at the entry step (pyruvate → acetyl-CoA) and again inside the cycle at α-ketoglutarate → succinyl-CoA. Blocking both is why the energy failure is so complete.
Image: Narayanese , WikiUserPedia , YassineMrabet , TotoBaggins — CC BY-SA 3.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Citric acid cycle with aconitate 2.svg

Why these structures — the lesion map

The lesions of Wernicke encephalopathy are strikingly stereotyped and bilaterally symmetric: mammillary bodies, medial (dorsomedial) thalamic nuclei, periaqueductal gray, tectal plate, the floor of the fourth ventricle, and the superior cerebellar vermis. The ASMBS review attributes this to "an inherently high rate of thiamine-dependent metabolism in these brain regions" — they are simply the tissue that runs its oxidative machinery hardest, sitting in a periventricular watershed. Learn the map and the physical exam writes itself.

Lesion site → lost function → clinical sign → how fast it comes back. This one figure explains the exam, the MRI, and the prognosis conversation.
Midsagittal dissection: find the mammillary body sitting just behind the optic chiasm at the base of the hypothalamus, with the fornix arcing over the thalamus toward it. Everything Wernicke damages clusters around the third ventricle and the aqueduct.
Image: John A Beal, PhD Dep't. of Cellular Biology & Anatomy, Louisiana State University Health Sciences Center Shreveport — CC BY 2.5. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Human brain left midsagitttal view closeup description 2.JPG
The corpus mamillare highlighted on the classic Gray's plate. Paired, tiny, and the structure most specifically injured in this disease — chronically they atrophy, which is the radiological fingerprint of established Korsakoff syndrome.
Image: MoraGre — CC0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Gray1180 Corpus Mamillare highlighted.png

Korsakoff syndrome — the same lesion, one step later

Wernicke encephalopathy is the acute event; Korsakoff syndrome is what is left behind when it is untreated or undertreated. The damage sits in the Papez circuit: hippocampus → fornix → mammillary body → mammillothalamic tract → anterior/dorsomedial thalamic nuclei → cingulate → back to hippocampus. Cut that loop and the patient can still perceive, converse, and reason — but can no longer lay down new episodic memory. The result is dense anterograde amnesia with a variable retrograde gradient, preserved procedural memory, and confabulation: the patient fills the gap with plausible narrative, not because they are lying, but because the monitoring system that would flag the gap is part of what was destroyed.

The memory circuit in three dimensions: hippocampus (red) → fornix (blue) → mammillary body (orange) → mammillothalamic tract (magenta) → anterior thalamic nuclei (yellow). Wernicke encephalopathy attacks the last three links at once.
Image: Mori S and Aggarwal M — CC BY 4.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Major gray and white matter limbic structures.jpg
The Papez circuit schematically. The ASMBS review localises Korsakoff to the anterior thalamic nucleus, mammillary bodies and corpus callosum, with reduced cortical glucose metabolism.
Image: NotMySecondOpinion — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Papez Circuit.jpg
Confabulation is not a lie and it is not a personality flaw. Do not "reality-orient" a confabulating Korsakoff patient by arguing — it does not work and it damages rapport. Redirect instead. And do not use confabulation to write the patient off: 56–84% of Wernicke patients progress to Korsakoff because they were not treated or were undertreated (ASMBS 2025). The patient in front of you may still be in the reversible window.

The glucose trap — why order of operations matters

A depleted patient has almost no TPP left. Give a dextrose load and you trigger a surge of glycolysis that consumes the last of it at the pyruvate dehydrogenase step — pyruvate is then shunted to lactate, ATP synthesis collapses in exactly the periventricular structures already on the edge, and clinical Wernicke encephalopathy is unmasked or sharply worsened. In thiamine-depleted rats, a glucose infusion produced medial thalamic acidosis, T2 hyperintensity and blood–brain barrier disruption within 40 minutes. EFNS states thiamine must be given "before any carbohydrate, because it is well known that glucose infusion precipitates WE in thiamine deficiency."

But get the nuance right, because people also err in the other direction. Schabelman & Kuo systematically reviewed this question and found 19 articles — 13 case reports or series, 4 animal studies, 2 expert opinions — with no evidence above the level of case report. Every human case involved prolonged or massive glucose (more than 2 L of 5% dextrose) without thiamine, or already-established Wernicke — not a single ampoule of D50. Their conclusion, verbatim: "a delay in giving glucose to hypoglycemic patients cannot be recommended at this time, although prompt thiamine supplementation after or concurrent with a return to normoglycemia is recommended." ASMBS 2025 agrees: "treatment of hypoglycemia should not be delayed for thiamine."

So, practically: hypoglycaemic and obtunded → give D50 now, and thiamine in the same breath or immediately after. Never let a dose of dextrose be held while pharmacy sends thiamine. Not hypoglycaemic, and about to start maintenance D5 fluids or feeds in a malnourished patient → thiamine goes in first. The FDA label for thiamine hydrochloride injection is explicit: patients with marginal thiamine status receiving dextrose should get 100 mg of thiamine in each of the first few litres of IV fluid.
Figure — why the order matters. Total body thiamine is never more than ~30 mg and can be exhausted in as little as 2 weeks of poor intake (ASMBS 2025; Frank, Adv Nutr 2015).

Route decides dose — why the tablet and the banana bag both fail

Thiamine crosses the gut through saturable, energy-dependent transporters (THTR-1/ThTR-2), and the ceiling is astonishingly low. In Thomson's classic studies, a single 20 mg oral dose delivered about 4.8 mg into a healthy subject — and only 1.5 mg into an alcoholic patient. Oral bioavailability of thiamine hydrochloride is roughly 3.7–5.3%. Alcohol compounds this by transcriptionally suppressing thiamine transporter-1. EFNS states the conclusion flatly: "orally administered thiamine hydrochloride is ineffective in increasing blood thiamine or curing WE." (The widely repeated "~4.5 mg absorption ceiling" traces back to a 2002 hypothesis rather than a measurement — Thomson's healthy-versus-alcoholic contrast above is the primary data, and it makes the point better anyway.)

There is one important refinement. Above the transporter's ceiling, thiamine also crosses by passive diffusion, which is not saturable — in a crossover study of 12 healthy volunteers, peak plasma levels rose from 40 to 95 to 385 nmol/L across 100 mg, 500 mg and 1500 mg oral doses. So very high oral doses can achieve meaningful blood levels. That makes 1500 mg/day orally a reasonable rescue when parenteral thiamine is genuinely unavailable — it does not make it a substitute for IV in acute Wernicke encephalopathy.

Figure — route and dose determine whether you are treating or merely documenting. Thiamine's plasma half-life of ~96 minutes is why divided dosing is preferred (StatPearls, NBK470344).
Thiamine hydrochloride. Pennies per dose, on every hospital formulary, and — at roughly 1 anaphylaxis per 5 million administrations — one of the safest interventions in medicine.
Image: Milda 444 — CC BY-SA 4.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Thiamin hydrochlorid.jpg
Axial midbrain: the cerebral aqueduct (2) ringed by the central gray stratum (3) — the periaqueductal gray. This ring, and the oculomotor nuclei within it, is what lights up on FLAIR and what produces the eye signs.
Image: Henry Vandyke Carter — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Gray710.png

Presentation — what you actually see

🔍

Signs & symptoms with frequency and mechanism

The classic triad is a trap. In Harper's 131 autopsy-proven cases the complete triad had been documented in only 16%, and 19% had no documented clinical signs at all. Even among diagnosed published cases the triad is present in about a third (32.7% pooled, 95% CI 19.2–47.7). If you wait for the triad you will miss most cases — and historically 80% of Wernicke–Korsakoff was never diagnosed during life.

Frequency colour key: >70% 40–70% 15–40% <15%. Read the two frequency columns carefully — they answer different questions. The autopsy column (Harper 1986) tells you how often a sign was actually documented in everyone who had the disease, including the many never recognised. The published-case column (EFNS 2010 pooled series) tells you how florid the picture is in patients who were diagnosed. The truth at the bedside sits between them.

Symptom / signAutopsy series

inattention, apathy, disorientation; family say "withdrawn" or "depressed"		 34–82%
usually quoted ~80%		 75.5% / 67.2% The most common presenting sign. Diffuse periventricular diencephalic energy failure with thalamic–medial temporal disconnection. Note how bland it is: the patient is quietly apathetic and inattentive, not agitated. That is exactly why it is charted as "intoxicated," "withdrawing," or "sundowning."

p<0.0001		 Brainstem oculomotor nuclei — the tissue with the least metabolic reserve in the brain. In Zuccoli's imaging cohort, 75% had ocular signs.

the single most common ocular sign		 majority of ocular cases Vestibular nuclei and the medial longitudinal fasciculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle fail, so the vestibulo-ocular reflex can no longer hold eccentric gaze — the eye drifts back and a fast phase corrects it. Hold lateral gaze for a full 10 seconds; a one-second glance will miss it.
⤷ Lateral rectus / CN VI palsy — usually bilateral, with horizontal diplopia and esotropia second most common The abducens nucleus sits in the floor of the fourth ventricle and drives the most ATP-expensive extraocular pair via a long thin axon. Bilateral abduction failure in a malnourished patient is Wernicke until proven otherwise.
⤷ Conjugate / vertical gaze palsy → complete ophthalmoplegia third; severe disease Periaqueductal gray, PPRF and the CN III/IV nuclei — the same tissue that lights up on FLAIR.
Gait ataxia — wide-based, truncal
"underreported… observing gait is inappropriately omitted from the neurological exam"		 ~23% 80.4% / 50.0%
p<0.0001		 Superior cerebellar vermis plus vestibular nuclei. Truncal and postural rather than limb ataxia — finger-to-nose can be normal while the patient cannot stand. Usually precedes the other signs by days to weeks. If you do not walk the patient, you will not find it.
Peripheral neuropathy (dry beriberi)
distal weakness, reduced reflexes, reduced vibration		 ~80%
of adults with thiamine deficiency		 Long axons cost the most ATP per cell and hold the least reserve, so they die back first; transketolase failure also starves myelin synthesis of NADPH and ribose. Can ascend and mimic Guillain–Barré. Usually already present and unnoticed — check ankle jerks and vibration on every at-risk patient.
Documented dietary deficiency a documentation artefact — 3.9% / 82.8%
p<0.0001		 This gap is not biology — it is behaviour. Clinicians simply do not record a nutrition history in people who drink. It is also a Caine criterion, so failing to ask actively lowers the score you would have calculated.
Mild memory impairment (as a Caine criterion) — 8.8% / 11.2% Early Papez-circuit involvement. Rarely tested formally in a confused patient, so under-captured.
Coma / severe depression of consciousness <5% Extensive brainstem and diencephalic involvement. Still reversible with prompt high-dose IV thiamine — severity is never a reason not to treat.
Seizures 0–3.1% Cortical involvement (an "atypical" pattern), which is more common in non-alcoholic Wernicke. Can be generalised, focal, or status.
Hearing loss / auditory dysfunction atypical Cochlear nuclei and medial geniculate. About 40% resolve within 2 weeks but roughly half retain some loss.
Hypothermia; postural hypotension, syncope, tachycardia rare Hypothalamic (posterior/preoptic) and dorsal vagal nucleus injury. Hypothermia in a confused malnourished patient is a classic under-recognised clue, routinely blamed on exposure or sepsis. (Published percentages for these two are review-level and could not be traced to a primary series — treat the numbers as soft, the association as real.)
Dysphagia under-recognised Nucleus ambiguus / medullary involvement. Matters enormously in practice: it is why these patients aspirate, and why a swallow evaluation belongs in the order set.
Cardiac failure — "wet beriberi" uncommon The same deficiency disables cardiac oxidative metabolism and causes peripheral vasodilation → high-output failure with tachycardia, raised CVP, oedema and sometimes pulmonary hypertension. Suspect it in warm shock with a wide pulse pressure and an unexplained lactate.
The three exam manoeuvres that most often make this diagnosis take about 90 seconds and are the three most often skipped: (1) hold lateral gaze for 10 full seconds looking for gaze-evoked nystagmus; (2) test abduction of each eye separately; (3) get the patient out of bed and watch them walk and turn a corner.

Alcohol-related vs non-alcoholic Wernicke — they do not look the same

Alcohol accounts for roughly 90–93% of Western hospitalised cases, and the hospitalisation rate is 14-fold higher than for non-alcoholic Wernicke (5.43 vs 0.39 per 100,000 person-years). But the non-alcoholic patient is the one you will miss — and they die more often for exactly that reason.

FeatureAlcohol-relatedNon-alcoholicWhat it means for you
Eye signs90.2%70.7%EFNS pooled published cases (alcoholic n = 102, non-alcoholic n = 116). The non-alcoholic patient presents as a quieter encephalopathy — you will not be handed the triad.
Cerebellar signs80.4%50.0%
Complete triad53.9%33.6%
Documented dietary deficiency3.9%82.8%Nobody records nutrition in drinkers.
VomitingLessMore (p<0.0001)Vomiting plus extreme weight loss are the strongest predictors of non-alcoholic Wernicke–Korsakoff.
In-hospital mortality3.2%8.5%Swiss national cohort, n = 4,393. Non-alcoholic patients die more because the diagnosis is made later.
Progression to Korsakoff (contemporary, treated)16.9%1.7%adjusted OR 10.64 (4.37–25.92). Alcohol adds ongoing neurotoxicity on top of the deficiency.
MRI patternClassic periventricular sites; contrast enhancement of mammillary bodies and thalamus is significantly associated with alcohol useAtypical sites are far more common — cerebellum, dentate, cranial nerve nuclei, red nuclei, caudate/putamen, splenium, fornix, cortexIn a post-bariatric or hyperemetic patient, "atypical" is the expected pattern. Do not let it dissuade you.
Two eras of numbers, and you should quote both. The classic figures — 17–20% mortality, Korsakoff in 80–85% of survivors — come from largely untreated, autopsy-era series. Contemporary cohorts with prompt thiamine report 5.1% pooled mortality (95% CI 2.3–8.8) and Korsakoff coded in 16.9% of alcohol-related admissions. The old numbers describe what this disease does when you miss it; the new ones describe what it does when you catch it. That difference is the treatment effect.

Who is at risk — the list you should be running in your head

When Wernicke is not alcohol-related, these are the causes, from the EFNS pooled series of 625 published non-alcoholic cases:

Alcohol use disorderAccounts for 90–93% of Western hospitalised cases. Up to 80% develop thiamine deficiency. WE lesions in 9.3% of AUD autopsies versus 1.3% otherwise; up to 59% of hospitalised alcohol-related deaths have WE at autopsy. AUD is present in up to 25% of hospitalised medical patients.Years of deficiency plus an acute precipitant — illness, a binge, withdrawal, or your bag of D5. Five additive mechanisms: reduced intake (calories from ethanol, poor diet); reduced absorption (a 20 mg oral dose delivers 4.8 mg to a healthy person but only 1.5 mg to an alcoholic patient, with transcriptional suppression of thiamine transporter-1); reduced hepatic storage; impaired phosphorylation to the active cofactor; and increased renal loss.
Bariatric & other GI surgery29% are already deficient before surgery; 25% after. Characteristic MRI lesions in only 14/30 (47%) of a post-bariatric cohort.79–94% present within 6 months; mean ~82 days; full reported range 1 day to 18 months. Risk is highest after malabsorptive operations (biliopancreatic diversion, Roux-en-Y gastric bypass) > sleeve or band — but it has occurred after every operation, after intragastric balloons, and after fad diets. Persistent post-op vomiting is the trigger.
GLP-1 / anti-obesity medicationsPublished case of WE from rapid weight loss on semaglutide; the ASMBS task force notes further unpublished cases.Rapid weight loss + nausea/vomiting + reduced intake. A genuinely new and growing risk group that has not yet reached most order sets.
Hyperemesis gravidarumHG affects 0.5–2.0% of pregnancies. In an 82-case review of HG-related WE: mean gestational age 16.5 ± 3 weeks. In 177 cases: subtherapeutic dosing in two-thirds, fetal loss 50%, maternal death 5%.WE followed a mean of 6.2 weeks of excessive vomiting where the fetus survived, versus 9 weeks where it did not. Usually late first / early second trimester. Almost always the admission where someone hangs dextrose without thiamine.
Critical illness / septic shock30–90% of critically ill patients are thiamine-deficient; up to 70% of ICU septic shock admissions.Can develop within 72 hours of acute illness with no intake — fever and sepsis raise requirement while intake is zero and renal/dialytic losses continue.
Malignancy / chemotherapyCancer is the single largest non-alcoholic category (18.1%). Thiamine deficiency in 55% of hospitalised oncology patients; 80% of those had a mental status abnormality.Anorexia, obstruction, emesis and raised demand. Specific culprits: 5-fluorouracil (its metabolite blocks the Krebs cycle and thiamine phosphate formation) and ifosfamide (a Wernicke-like encephalopathy).
Dialysis (HD or PD)Thiamine is water-soluble and dialysable — plasma levels fall by ~50% in some HD patients. In one report of 9 dialysis-dependent WE cases, 7 were diagnosed post-mortem.Insidious, or acute after HD initiation. Give thiamine after the session so you are not simply dialysing it off.
Anorexia nervosa & restrictive eatingThiamine deficiency in about 38% of patients with anorexia nervosa.Weeks of restriction, then unmasked at refeeding — a double hit.
Refeeding, any cause—Days after nutrition restarts. The carbohydrate load consumes whatever thiamine is left, exactly as a dextrose bolus does.
Parenteral nutrition without multivitamins—Days to weeks. Historic US multivitamin-infusion shortages caused fatal Wernicke encephalopathy — a genuine, recurring drug-supply hazard.
Type 2 diabetesThiamine levels 50–75% lower than in people without diabetes, probably from increased renal clearance (worse with albuminuria).Then add metformin, which reduces the ThTR-2 intestinal transporter, and repeated glucose loads.
Heart failureBoth a consequence (wet beriberi) and a cause. One study: 300 mg/day orally for 28 days improved LVEF by 30%.Loop diuretics have long been thought to increase urinary thiamine loss — this is genuinely contested: a study of 73 patients over 65 found no association with furosemide. Say "possible," not "established."
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass — the most frequently implicated operation. The duodenum and proximal jejunum, where thiamine is absorbed, are bypassed entirely, on top of a small pouch and frequent post-operative vomiting.

The rest of the deficiency — beriberi

Wernicke encephalopathy is the neurologic face of thiamine deficiency. The same deficiency produces three other syndromes, and the FDA label for thiamine hydrochloride injection lists them as formal indications:

SyndromeFeatures — and the trap
Dry beriberiSymmetric distal sensorimotor axonal peripheral neuropathy with reduced proprioception and foot drop. Can ascend and mimic Guillain–Barré — the discriminator is the nutrition history and the absence of albuminocytologic dissociation.
Wet beriberiHigh-output cardiac failure with peripheral vasodilation: tachycardia, elevated CVP, systemic congestion, peripheral oedema, sometimes pulmonary hypertension. The echo shows a hyperdynamic ventricle, not a failing one — which is why it gets called "not cardiac."
Shoshin beriberiFulminant decompensated cardiac beriberi: shock with a high lactate and metabolic acidosis, abdominal pain, anorexia, sometimes hypothermia. Mimics septic shock — warm, vasodilated, high output — but responds to IV thiamine rather than to antibiotics and pressors. See the ICU panel.
Gastrointestinal beriberiAbdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, gastroparesis and ileus with an alarmingly elevated lactate. Untreated, it commonly progresses to Wernicke encephalopathy — and the vomiting deepens the deficiency that caused it.
Wet beriberi: generalised oedema below the waist with the "air hunger" facies of high-output failure. A historical plate — the physiology is unchanged; today's patient is a post-bariatric or ICU patient rather than a sailor.
Image: W. Hamilton Jefferys — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Heart failure in wet beriberi.jpg
Dry beriberi: late-stage distal paralysis with wasting. The same axonal die-back you detect early, and cheaply, as absent ankle reflexes and reduced vibration sense.
Image: W. Hamilton Jefferys — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Late stage of paralysis with atrophy in dry beriberi.jpg
