Making the diagnosis

🧭

Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis

There is no test that rules this in or out in time to matter. A whole-blood thiamine level takes about 4 days to return, and once you have given thiamine it will be normal regardless. MRI misses roughly half of cases. Treat on suspicion. ASMBS 2025 puts it as an explicit recommendation: "Draw labs and treat simultaneously" and "treat before or in the absence of labs."

Caine criteria — the operational definition

The classic triad is too insensitive to use. The Caine criteria (Caine et al., JNNP 1997), validated against 106 autopsies, require only two of four features and achieve 85% sensitivity. They are the criteria named in the ASMBS 2025 recommendations and are what you should actually be applying at the bedside.

Caine criteria for Wernicke encephalopathy — interactive

Select every feature present. Two or more = Caine-positive.

①
Dietary deficiency
History of poor intake, weight loss, vomiting, malabsorption, alcohol use disorder, bariatric surgery, dialysis, or any state of increased thiamine demand.
②
Oculomotor abnormality
Nystagmus (esp. gaze-evoked), ophthalmoplegia or ophthalmoparesis, CN VI palsy, conjugate gaze palsy.
③
Cerebellar dysfunction
Gait or truncal ataxia, unsteadiness, past-pointing, dysdiadochokinesia. You must watch them walk.
④
Altered mental state OR mild memory impairment
Confusion, inattention, apathy, disorientation, or impaired recall on formal testing.
0
of 4 criteria present
Source: Caine D, Halliday GM, Kril JJ, Harper CG. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 1997;62:51–60 — operational criteria derived and validated on 106 autopsy-confirmed alcoholic cases, with 100% inter- and intra-rater reliability across three independent raters. The 2-of-4 rule gives ~85% sensitivity and 100% specificity in that cohort, versus roughly 22% sensitivity for insisting on the complete triad. A negative score does not exclude the diagnosis in a high-risk patient — when in doubt, treat.
Two caveats about Caine that are routinely forgotten. First, the criteria were derived and validated in chronic alcoholics — in a post-bariatric or hyperemetic patient they are a useful prompt, not a validated rule. Second, their performance degrades in the presence of hepatic encephalopathy, and approaches 100% sensitivity only in alcoholic patients without it. Since hepatic encephalopathy is the commonest reason Wernicke gets missed, the criteria are weakest exactly where you need them most. Treat empirically in that setting rather than scoring your way out of it.

Laboratory workup — what to send, and how to read it

Nothing here confirms the diagnosis. You are sending labs to find the company Wernicke keeps (hypomagnesemia, refeeding electrolytes, liver disease) and to exclude mimics.

TestWhen / whyHow to interpret it — and what fools you
Magnesium do not skipOn arrival, before or with the first thiamine dose, then daily.Mg²⁺ is a required cofactor both for converting thiamine → TPP and for transketolase itself. Hypomagnesemia produces thiamine-refractory Wernicke — the patient who "isn't responding to thiamine" very often has a magnesium of 1.2. Serum Mg underestimates total body stores (only ~1% is extracellular), so a low-normal value in a malnourished drinker still warrants repletion. Falsely raised by hemolysis; lowered by alcohol, diuretics, PPIs, diarrhoea and refeeding.
Whole-blood thiamine (thiamine diphosphate, TDP)
reference ~70–180 nmol/L		Draw before the first dose if the tube is already in your hand — but never delay treatment for it. Specimen: 2 mL EDTA whole blood, protected from light.The most specific assay available, and still frequently normal in genuine Wernicke because blood levels do not reflect brain levels. Turnaround is 3–6 days and can reach 14, against a therapeutic window of hours. A single dose of thiamine invalidates the result, so follow-up levels are explicitly not recommended. This is a documentation and audit tool, not a decision tool. If the tube is not in your hand within 60 seconds, give the thiamine.
Erythrocyte transketolase activity (± TPP effect / activation coefficient)Rarely available; the historical functional assay, now largely replaced by direct HPLC thiamine measurement.Measures enzyme activity before and after adding TPP in vitro; a large increment implies deficiency. Bands: TPP effect 0–15% normal, 15–25% marginal, >25% deficient. Confounded by anaemia, recent transfusion, and — again — by magnesium status.
Phosphate, potassiumBaseline and at least daily through the first 72 h of feeding.The refeeding triad. Once you restart calories, insulin drives phosphate, potassium and magnesium intracellularly along with thiamine. A falling phosphate on day 2 of feeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise.
Lactate / VBGIf shock, tachypnoea, or an unexplained anion gap.Pyruvate dehydrogenase blockade shunts pyruvate to lactate, so thiamine deficiency is a genuine cause of type B lactic acidosis — a lactate that does not fit the perfusion state. Also the signature of Shoshin beriberi. Raised falsely by tourniquet time and by hepatic clearance failure.
Glucose (POC, immediately)Before any dextrose is hung.Drives the order of operations. If genuinely hypoglycaemic, treat it — but give thiamine at the same time.
CMP, LFTs, INR, albumin, prealbuminAdmission.Establishes concurrent alcohol-associated liver disease, which changes benzodiazepine choice and complicates the mental-status differential. Low albumin marks the malnutrition, not the cause of it.
AmmoniaOnly if cirrhosis or portal hypertension is plausible.Helps separate hepatic encephalopathy — but ammonia is notoriously unreliable (falsely high with tourniquet use, delayed transport to the lab, a warm sample, or muscle activity). Never use a normal ammonia to exclude Wernicke, and never use a high one to exclude it either — the two coexist constantly.
Ethanol level, urine drug screenAdmission in any AUD presentation.A confused patient with an ethanol of zero and a history of daily drinking is heading into withdrawal and may be Wernicke. The two diagnoses are not alternatives.
CBC, B12, folateAdmission in malnutrition.Macrocytosis is common in AUD from alcohol itself, folate deficiency, and liver disease. B12 deficiency produces its own myelopathy/neuropathy and is a co-traveller, especially post-bariatric.
TSH, HIV, RPRWhen the picture is atypical or risk factors exist.Hypothyroidism increases thiamine requirements and independently causes cognitive slowing; HIV and neurosyphilis are important mimics of subacute encephalopathy.
CKFound-down, prolonged immobility, seizure.Rhabdomyolysis is common in this population and drives AKI, which then complicates fluid and electrolyte management.

Imaging — helpful when positive, worthless when negative

MRI sensitivity
53%
Antunez 1998, reaffirmed by EFNS (Class II). ASMBS quotes 52–65%; a modern series with FLAIR reached 77%
MRI specificity
93%
PPV 89% — a positive study is close to diagnostic
Head CT sensitivity
13%
2 of 15 acute cases showed any abnormality — order CT to exclude bleed, never to find Wernicke
Best single sequence
FLAIR
36/47 positive studies; order MRI with and without contrast if renal function allows
A roughly 47% false-negative rate means a normal MRI changes nothing about your management. EFNS recommends MRI to support the diagnosis (Level B) — not to make or exclude it. And acute signal change can normalise within 2 days of starting thiamine, so a scan obtained late is negative for the best possible reason.

Where the lesions actually are — Zuccoli 2009, n = 56

Site% of patientsWhat it produces clinically
Medial thalami + periventricular third ventricle80%Confusion, inattention, and — via the anterior nuclei — the amnesia of Korsakoff
Periaqueductal gray59%Gaze palsies, vertical gaze failure
Mammillary bodies45%Memory; the site of the classic petechial haemorrhage and of chronic atrophy
Tectal plate36%Vertical gaze and pupillary abnormalities
Periventricular gray anterior to the fourth ventricle7%Nystagmus, CN VI palsy — clinically loud but radiologically quiet
FindingSequence & siteWhat it means and when it appears
Symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity — medial (dorsomedial) thalamiAxial FLAIR/T2, at the level of the third ventricleThe commonest positive finding. Bilateral symmetry is the key discriminator from stroke. Corresponds to the cytotoxic + vasogenic edema of the cascade; usually resolves after successful thiamine replacement.
Symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity — periaqueductal gray and tectal plateAxial FLAIR at the midbrainThe anatomic correlate of the eye signs. Ring of signal around the cerebral aqueduct.
Mammillary body signal change ± contrast enhancementCoronal T1 post-gadolinium; thin slicesEnhancement of the mammillary bodies and thalamus is regarded as near-pathognomonic and was significantly associated with alcohol abuse in Zuccoli's series; it is seen in roughly half of patients overall. It reflects blood–brain barrier breakdown. Easy to miss if the radiologist is not told the question — write "?Wernicke — please assess mammillary bodies and periaqueductal gray" on the requisition. Mammillary body signal change is independently associated with short-term memory loss (OR 2.2).
Restricted diffusion (DWI bright, ADC dark)DWI/ADCCytotoxic edema from Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase failure. Its presence in a symmetric periventricular distribution is characteristic; unlike arterial stroke it does not respect a vascular territory.
Floor of the fourth ventricle / vestibular and abducens nucleiAxial FLAIR at the ponsCorrelates with nystagmus and abduction failure.
Atypical sites — cerebellum and dentate nuclei, cranial nerve nuclei, red nuclei, caudate/putamen, splenium, fornix, cerebral cortex, dorsal medulla, pons, substantia nigraAnywhereZuccoli found atypical signal only in non-alcoholic patients and always alongside typical findings. A 2024 series tempers that absolute — atypical changes in 23% overall (21% of alcoholics, 67% of non-alcoholics) — but the direction holds. In a post-bariatric or hyperemetic patient, atypical is the expected pattern; do not let it dissuade you. Cortical involvement carries a poorer prognosis.
Mammillary body and midbrain tegmentum atrophyCoronal T1, chronic phaseThe radiological signature of established Korsakoff syndrome, with third-ventricle dilatation and generalised atrophy. Atrophic change can appear as early as one week. This is damage, not oedema — it does not reverse.
Axial FLAIR — medial dorsal thalami. Bilateral, symmetric, periventricular hyperintensity flanking the third ventricle. This is the single most recognisable image in Wernicke encephalopathy.
Image: Jto410 — CC BY-SA 3.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · MRI FLAIR sequence Wernicke Encephalopathy.jpg
Axial FLAIR — periaqueductal gray and tectum. A collar of signal around the cerebral aqueduct. Compare with the anatomic midbrain section in the pathophysiology section above.
Image: Jto410 — CC BY-SA 3.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · MRI FLAIR sequence showing hyperintense signal in the periaqueducal grey matter in Wernicke Encephalopathy.jpg
DWI — restricted diffusion, mesial dorsal thalami. Cytotoxic edema. Symmetric and crossing vascular territories, which is how you separate it from bilateral thalamic infarction (artery of Percheron).
Image: Jto410 — CC BY-SA 3.0. Source: Wikimedia Commons · MRI DWI sequence showing restricted diffusion in the mesial dorsal thalami.jpg
The anatomy for reference. Cerebral aqueduct (2) surrounded by central gray stratum (3), with the oculomotor nuclei embedded in it — precisely the tissue that becomes hyperintense.
Image: Henry Vandyke Carter — Public domain. Source: Wikimedia Commons · Gray710.png
MRI has a prognostic role even though it is a poor diagnostic one. In a review of 34 cases, patients who recovered early (within 4 weeks) had a lower incidence of T2/FLAIR abnormality at the typical sites — and less cerebellar ataxia — than those who recovered late.

Differential diagnosis — and why "both" is usually the right answer

MimicWhat points away from WernickeThe trap
Alcohol withdrawal / delirium tremensHyperadrenergic: tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, agitation, hallucinations, 48–96 h after the last drink.Wernicke is typically quiet and apathetic. They coexist constantly — and benzodiazepines will sedate your patient and erase the mental-status exam you needed. Treat both.
Hepatic encephalopathyAsterixis, stigmata of cirrhosis, precipitant (bleed, infection, constipation), response to lactulose.Ophthalmoplegia and nystagmus are not features of HE. If the eyes are abnormal, think Wernicke — and remember the two share a patient population almost perfectly.
Bilateral thalamic infarct (artery of Percheron)Abrupt onset, vascular risk factors, often vertical gaze palsy with hypersomnolence; DWI respects the perforator territory.Both are symmetric and thalamic. Wernicke also involves periaqueductal gray and mammillary bodies; stroke usually does not.
Subdural haematomaFocal deficit, headache, fall history, anticoagulation.Same population (falls + coagulopathy). Get the CT — but give the thiamine while you wait.
CNS infection (meningitis, encephalitis)Fever, meningismus, CSF pleocytosis, seizures.Sepsis itself causes thiamine deficiency in up to 70% of ICU admissions — these are additive, not exclusive.
HypoglycaemiaResolves with glucose.The correction itself can precipitate Wernicke. Give thiamine alongside.
Hyponatraemia / osmotic demyelinationSodium trajectory; ODS gives locked-in or pontine signs days after overcorrection.Malnourished patients are exquisitely vulnerable to both. Correct sodium slowly in this population.
Miller Fisher syndrome / Bickerstaff encephalitisAreflexia, anti-GQ1b antibodies, antecedent infection.Ophthalmoplegia + ataxia is the shared signature. Nutrition history decides it.
Non-convulsive status epilepticusEEG.Both look like unexplained persistent confusion. If AMS does not improve in 24–48 h of full-dose thiamine, get an EEG.
Metronidazole-induced encephalopathyDrug exposure; MRI shows dentate nucleus and splenium lesions.Metronidazole is a thiamine analogue that can cause a functional deficiency even with normal thiamine levels — so it may be causing both pictures at once.
B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, HIV, neurosyphilis, CJD, normal-pressure hydrocephalus, Marchiafava–BignamiEach has its own signature (posterior column signs, myxoedema, serology, myoclonus/EEG, gait–urinary–cognitive triad, corpus callosum lesions).Several travel with the same malnutrition. Screen broadly; treat thiamine first.
Ex juvantibus — treatment as a diagnostic test. Symptoms usually begin improving within 24–48 hours of high-dose IV thiamine, and the ocular signs are the fastest to move, often within hours. Document the eye exam before your first dose and re-examine at 6–12 h: resolution of nystagmus or of an abduction deficit is powerful confirmation. Failure to respond should send you looking for hypomagnesemia first, then for a second diagnosis.
🩺 Clinic — prevention, recognition & the long game
Assess

When to suspect it in clinic

🔍

What it looks like before it becomes an emergency

Clinic is where this disease is prevented, and occasionally where it is caught early enough that the patient still walks out with their memory. The presentation here is subtle: not a florid triad, but a post-bariatric patient six weeks out who is still vomiting; a pregnant patient in week 14 who has lost weight; a patient on semaglutide who has stopped eating; a heavy drinker whose family says they seem "vague."

Presentation in clinicWhat to do about it today
Post-bariatric patient with persistent vomiting or weight loss beyond expectationThe single highest-yield scenario. Most post-bariatric Wernicke occurs in the first 3–4 months, and 79–94% within 6 months. Persistent vomiting is the trigger. Do not wait for neurological signs — treat the deficiency and check for a mechanical cause.
Pregnancy with prolonged hyperemesisWernicke followed a mean of 6.2 weeks of excessive vomiting where the fetus survived and 9 weeks where it did not. If vomiting has run for weeks, thiamine goes in before any dextrose-containing fluid.
New or worsening unsteadiness in a drinkerAtaxia usually precedes the other signs by days to weeks. Walk them down the corridor. A new wide-based gait is a reason to send to the ED, not to book a follow-up.
Family reports the patient is "withdrawn," "vague," or "depressed"This is how the altered mental status of early Wernicke is described by families. Test recall after a delay and examine the eyes before you reach for an antidepressant.
Rapid weight loss on a GLP-1 receptor agonistAn emerging, under-recognised cause. Ask about intake, not just weight. Consider prophylactic thiamine in anyone with poor intake or persistent nausea.
Unexplained peripheral neuropathy in a malnourished patientDry beriberi. Around 80% of adults with thiamine deficiency have some degree of neuropathy — it is often the earliest objective sign, and it is free to find with a tuning fork and a reflex hammer.
Do not attempt to treat suspected Wernicke encephalopathy in clinic. Oral thiamine cannot do it — a 20 mg oral dose delivers about 4.8 mg to a healthy person and only 1.5 mg to someone who drinks, and EFNS states plainly that oral thiamine hydrochloride "is ineffective in increasing blood thiamine or curing WE." If you suspect it, the patient goes to the emergency department today for parenteral treatment. Give a dose of oral thiamine on the way out if you have it, but do not let it substitute for the referral.
Prevent

Prophylactic thiamine — who, and how much

💊

The doses that keep people out of the hospital

PRIMARY PREVENTION — ASMBS Wernicke's Task Force 2025
100 mg PO daily, starting ≥2 weeks before weight-loss treatment→ continue while on medication and ≥3 months after surgery→ ≥12 mg PO daily indefinitely

The task force's framing is worth borrowing on rounds: Wernicke encephalopathy "is clinically comparable to venous thromboembolism in that they are both low-prevalence, high-risk conditions — but VTE prevention has become routine in medicine, in contrast to WE prophylaxis, which is more likely to be overlooked."

SettingStartContinueLong-term targetWhy this dose
Before bariatric surgery or an anti-obesity medication Thiamine 100 mg PO daily, beginning at least 2 weeks before starting Throughout treatment and for at least 3 months after surgery At least 12 mg/day indefinitely; preferably 50 mg once or twice daily to keep blood levels normal Up to 29% of patients are already thiamine-deficient before surgery — partly because of the high-carbohydrate and pre-operative liquid diets. Starting on the day of surgery is starting too late.
Routine post-bariatric maintenance Bariatric-specific multivitamin Lifelong Minimum 12 mg/day, preferably 50 mg once or twice daily A typical over-the-counter multivitamin contains only about 1.5 mg of thiamine — an order of magnitude short. Adult parenteral multivitamin infusions contain 6 mg per daily dose; adult enteral formula 2.2–2.9 mg per 1500 kcal. None of these constitutes prophylaxis for a bypassed duodenum.
Alcohol use disorder, ambulatory Thiamine 100 mg PO daily (some sources use 100 mg PO three times daily for low-risk prophylaxis) Ongoing while drinking continues Continue indefinitely; add a multivitamin and folate 1 mg Cheap, safe, and the only thing standing between chronic marginal deficiency and the next hospitalisation. Recognise its limits: absorption is halved by alcohol, so this reduces risk — it does not eliminate it, and it will not treat an acute episode.
Hyperemesis gravidarum Thiamine supplementation with every admission, and before any dextrose-containing IV fluid Until vomiting resolves and intake is adequate Prenatal vitamin; RDA in pregnancy is 1.4 mg/day In a series of 177 pregnancy-related Wernicke cases, two-thirds received a subtherapeutic dose, fetal loss was 50% and maternal death 5%. Under-dosing, not failure to think of it, is the documented failure mode.
Dialysis Daily oral thiamine as part of a renal vitamin Ongoing — Thiamine is water-soluble and dialysable. Give it after the session so you are not simply dialysing it back off.
Any patient starting nutrition after a period of starvation Thiamine before the first calories Through the refeeding period — The carbohydrate load of refeeding consumes residual thiamine exactly as a dextrose bolus does. This applies to a tray of food as much as to TPN.
Post-bariatric surveillance. ASMBS's 2017 nutrition guidelines recommend pre-operative whole-blood thiamine testing for all weight-loss-surgery patients, and the 2020 clinical practice guidelines recommend screening for thiamine deficiency in high-risk patients — those with malnutrition, rapid weight loss, or GI symptoms such as intractable nausea, vomiting or constipation. The 2025 task force adds: follow levels for 6 months after surgery, and treat before or in the absence of labs.
Who counts as "high risk" post-operatively? ASMBS defines it concretely: persistent vomiting, or sudden and severe weight loss greater than the typical early post-operative loss — roughly 8% of total body weight at 3 weeks after surgery. Those patients need parenteral, not oral, repletion.
Screen

USPSTF A & B recommendations for this population

🛡️

The screening that actually applies

GradeRecommendationPopulation & how
B Screen for unhealthy alcohol use and provide brief behavioural counselling interventions to those engaged in risky or hazardous drinking (2018) Adults 18 years or older, including pregnant people. Use the AUDIT-C (3 questions, 1–2 minutes; positive at ≥4 for men, ≥3 for women) or the single alcohol screening question (days in the past year with 5+ drinks for men, 4+ for women and adults over 65). This is the single most relevant preventive service to Wernicke encephalopathy that exists.

Update pending: a draft USPSTF recommendation posted 5 August 2025 retains Grade B for adults ≥18 including pregnancy, and Grade I (insufficient evidence) for adolescents 12–17. A published final version could not be confirmed as of July 2026 — cite the 2018 Grade B and note the pending update. Additional USPSTF screening applies to this population: tobacco cessation, hepatitis C, hepatitis B, HIV, depression and intimate partner violence are all relevant to people with alcohol use disorder or malnutrition. Grades and population wording change, so check the current statement at uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org rather than relying on memory.

AUDIT-C — the three-question alcohol screen

Items reproduced verbatim from the VA AUDIT-C form (v3.0, 2013), which references the WHO AUDIT Guidelines, 2nd ed. Takes 1–2 minutes.

0
AUDIT-C score (range 0–12)
Bush K, Kivlahan DR, McDonell MB, Fihn SD, Bradley KA. Arch Intern Med 1998;158:1789–95 — in 243 male VA general-medicine patients, a cutoff of ≥4 gave 86% sensitivity and 72% specificity for heavy drinking and/or active abuse or dependence (+LR 3.07); a cutoff of ≥3 identified 90% with active abuse/dependence and 98% of heavy drinkers but with only 60% specificity. The women's ≥3 threshold comes from Bradley KA et al., Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2007;31:1208–17.

Two caveats. In question 2, both "None, I do not drink" and "1 or 2" score zero — an easy scoring error. And the VA operational threshold differs from the published one: VA treats ≥5 as positive for both sexes and requires documentation of brief counselling, with severity bands 0–3 low-risk, 4–5 moderate, 6–7 high, 8–12 severe. Say which cutoff you are using. The original validation cohort was predominantly white male veterans with a mean age of 67.
Screening for unhealthy alcohol use is a Grade B service — at least moderate certainty of moderate net benefit, and covered without cost-sharing under the ACA. It takes under two minutes. In a disease where 90–93% of Western hospitalised cases are alcohol-related and prevention costs pennies, this is the highest-leverage two minutes in the visit.
Treat

Treating the cause — alcohol use disorder

🍺

Pharmacotherapy — first line and escalation

Wernicke encephalopathy in an alcohol-using patient is a sentinel event. Treating the episode without treating the alcohol use disorder guarantees the sequel: one-year readmission after alcohol-related Wernicke is 31.6%. Start pharmacotherapy in hospital, not at a follow-up appointment the patient will not remember to attend.

The two major guidelines disagree about first line — know both. VA/DoD 2021 gives a strong recommendation for naltrexone (oral or extended-release) or topiramate, and only a weak recommendation for acamprosate or disulfiram, with gabapentin reserved for when first-line agents fail. APA 2018 puts naltrexone or acamprosate first (1B), with disulfiram, topiramate or gabapentin as second-line (2C). Either answer is defensible on rounds — but say which guideline you are quoting.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / maxWhy it works & when to pick itLimits, alternatives & monitoring
Naltrexone PO first line 50 mg PO daily, or 25 mg once–twice daily with food during week 1 to limit nausea Step from 25 mg to 50 mg after about a week if tolerated 50–100 mg daily (COMBINE used up to 100 mg) µ-opioid antagonist — blocks the endogenous-opioid-mediated dopamine surge that makes drinking rewarding. Reduces heavy-drinking days. Strong recommendation in VA/DoD 2021; 1B in APA 2018. Contraindicated in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure and in anyone using opioids — must be opioid-free 7–14 days (including tramadol), or you will precipitate withdrawal. Baseline LFTs, GGT, bilirubin and β-hCG; recheck LFTs at 6 months, then yearly. The old hepatotoxicity boxed warning has been removed but the contraindication stands. If contraindicated → acamprosate.
Naltrexone XR (IM) 380 mg deep IM gluteal No titration 380 mg every 4 weeks, alternating buttocks Identical mechanism, but removes daily adherence from the equation — which matters enormously in a patient with memory impairment. This is often the right choice after Wernicke. Same opioid caveat; discontinue for acute hepatitis. CrCl <50: use with caution, no dose adjustment. Needs adequate gluteal muscle mass. The label expects the patient to be able to abstain in an outpatient setting before initiation.
Acamprosate best in liver disease 666 mg PO three times daily (two 333 mg delayed-release tablets per dose) No titration — start at target 1,998 mg/day Modulates glutamatergic and GABAergic tone back toward balance during abstinence, damping the protracted hyperexcitability that drives relapse. No hepatic metabolism — the agent of choice when the liver is bad, which in this population is often. CrCl 30–50: reduce to 333 mg PO TID. CrCl ≤30: contraindicated. Reduce if under 60 kg. Works best if the patient is already ≥4 days abstinent. Three-times-daily pill burden is the real-world failure point in an amnestic patient. Baseline creatinine clearance and β-hCG.
Topiramate off-label 25 mg PO daily Increase by 25–50 mg/day, divided BID, at weekly intervals 200–300 mg/day Strong recommendation in VA/DoD 2021 (second-line in APA 2018). Reduces glutamatergic drive and dopaminergic reward signalling. CrCl <70: give 50% of the dose. Teratogenic (cleft lip/palate) and reduces hormonal contraceptive levels. Nephrolithiasis, metabolic acidosis (check bicarbonate), acute angle-closure glaucoma, paraesthesia, weight loss. If side effects persist beyond 4–6 weeks, reduce the dose. Dose-dependent cognitive and word-finding impairment makes this a poor choice right after Wernicke — see the caution below.
Gabapentin off-label 300 mg PO at bedtime Increase by 300 mg/day in divided doses as tolerated 1,800 mg/day in three divided doses Reserved for when first-line agents are contraindicated or ineffective (VA/DoD 2021 weak-for; APA 2018 2C). Benefit is concentrated in patients with high baseline withdrawal symptoms — at 1,800 mg/day, number needed to treat was 8 for abstinence and 5 for no heavy drinking. CrCl 30–59: 400–1,400 mg/day in 2 divided doses. CrCl 15–29: 200–700 mg at bedtime. Misuse and diversion potential; additive CNS depression with opioids and benzodiazepines. Causes sedation and ataxia — which directly confounds the Wernicke exam you are following.
Disulfiram Up to 500 mg daily × 1–2 weeks (initial phase) Step down after the initial phase 250 mg daily (range 125–500 mg); never exceed 500 mg/day Aversive, not anti-craving: blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase so that drinking produces a toxic acetaldehyde reaction. Only works in a motivated, abstinence-committed patient with supervised administration. Not recommended in alcohol-associated liver disease — hepatically metabolised and hepatotoxic; contraindicated in severe hepatic dysfunction, severe myocardial disease or coronary occlusion, and psychosis. Patient must be abstinent ≥12 h before starting, and the reaction can occur up to 14 days after the last dose. Do not give metronidazole within 2 weeks (psychosis). Baseline LFTs, CBC, BMP, ECG, β-hCG; LFTs at 1 month, then monthly × 3, then periodically. Can itself cause peripheral neuropathy — unhelpful in a patient who already has one.
Baclofen ACG 2024 first line in compensated ALD 10 mg PO three times daily (the RCT dose in alcohol-associated cirrhosis) Per response and sedation 30 mg/day in the trial regimen GABA-B agonist. ACG 2024 gives baclofen a strong recommendation (moderate evidence) for alcohol use disorder in compensated alcohol-associated liver disease — a genuinely under-known recommendation, and highly relevant here since so many of these patients have liver disease. Renally cleared — reduce in chronic kidney disease. Patients with hepatic encephalopathy were excluded from the trial and it may impair mentation, so avoid it if HE is in the picture. Sedating.
Choosing the agent after a Wernicke episode — the consideration nobody writes down. You are going to be serially examining this patient's cognition, gait and eye movements for weeks to judge recovery. The two agents most likely to blur that picture are topiramate (dose-dependent cognitive and word-finding impairment) and gabapentin (sedation and ataxia). Naltrexone and acamprosate are the cleaner choices in a patient recovering from Wernicke — and acamprosate is the safest if the liver is bad. (This is clinical synthesis from the labelled adverse-effect profiles, not a cited guideline recommendation.)
Two things APA 2018 says not to do. Do not use antidepressants for alcohol use disorder in the absence of a co-occurring indication (1B), and do not use benzodiazepines except for acute withdrawal or a separate indication (1C). Both are commonly prescribed by reflex in this population, and both are wrong on their own.
ACG 2024 on nutrition in alcohol-associated liver disease — Key Concept 25: "Thiamine, vitamin B12, and zinc deficiencies are common in individuals with alcohol-associated hepatitis and should be supplemented," noting that supplementing thiamine may help prevent Wernicke encephalopathy. The guideline's caloric goal is 35 kcal/kg/day with 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day of protein.
Investigational — ask, don't prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists for alcohol use disorder. A 2026 randomised trial of semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly in 108 patients with alcohol use disorder and obesity reduced heavy-drinking days by 41.1 percentage points versus 26.4 with placebo (treatment difference −13.7 pp, 95% CI −22.0 to −5.4, p = 0.0015), and a 2025 trial (n = 48) reduced laboratory alcohol self-administration and craving. No guideline — VA/DoD, APA, ASAM, AASLD or ACG — currently recommends GLP-1 receptor agonists for alcohol use disorder, and a phase 3 trial is under way. Note the irony worth flagging to patients: these same drugs are themselves an emerging cause of Wernicke encephalopathy through rapid weight loss and vomiting.
Monitor

Follow-up after a Wernicke episode

📈

Cadence and what to check

WhenWhat to do
Within 1–2 weeks of dischargeIn person, not by phone. Confirm the patient is actually taking thiamine 300 mg two to three times daily. Repeat the eye and gait exam and compare with the discharge documentation. Test delayed recall — this is when an emerging Korsakoff syndrome becomes visible as the acute confusion clears.
Monthly for the first 3 monthsASMBS reports a high incidence of recurrent Wernicke after discharge and advises reassessing frequently in person, because relapse may need readmission and another course of high-dose IV thiamine. Re-check magnesium, phosphate and potassium; review weight and intake.
Post-bariatric patientsFollow thiamine levels for 6 months after surgery, alongside the standard micronutrient panel. Any return of vomiting resets the clock.
OngoingContinue thiamine 300 mg two to three times daily until the risk factors resolve, then 100 mg daily indefinitely. Maintain alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy and continue brief interventions at every visit.
ReferralsNeurology if signs fail to improve or the diagnosis is uncertain. Neuropsychology for formal memory testing before any capacity or return-to-work decision. Addiction medicine — early, and started in hospital rather than promised at follow-up. PT/OT for residual ataxia and neuropathy. Dietitian, especially post-bariatric.
Capacity and driving. A patient with Korsakoff syndrome converses normally, agrees with the plan, and will not remember it. Assess capacity by testing recall of the plan after a delay, and corroborate everything with a family member. Someone must explicitly address driving: amnesia plus residual ataxia plus peripheral neuropathy is not a safe combination behind the wheel, and "nobody raised it" is how it goes unaddressed for years.
Escalate

When to send to the ED

🚑

Red flags — same day, not next week

Send to the emergency department today, for parenteral thiamine, if an at-risk patient has any of:
  • Any new eye finding — gaze-evoked nystagmus, an abduction deficit, diplopia, or a gaze palsy
  • A new wide-based or unsteady gait, or inability to walk unaided
  • New confusion, inattention, apathy, or impaired delayed recall
  • Two or more Caine criteria (see the calculator in the diagnosis section)
  • Persistent vomiting with weight loss after bariatric surgery, or several weeks of hyperemesis in pregnancy
  • Inability to tolerate oral intake, so that oral thiamine is not even a theoretical option
  • Hypothermia, unexplained hypotension, or syncope in a malnourished patient
Call ahead and say the words. Tell the emergency department you are sending a patient with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy who needs high-dose IV thiamine — 500 mg IV, before any dextrose. A referral that says "confusion, please assess" gets a banana bag and a CT head. Naming the diagnosis and the dose is the intervention.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

Every patient with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy is admitted. There is no outpatient pathway for treating it: the treatment is parenteral, it runs for at least 5 days, and the differential includes several things that kill people overnight. The real triage decision is floor versus ICU.

Admit to the floorStraight to ICU — see the ICU panel
  • Caine-positive (≥2 of 4), or any at-risk patient with new confusion, eye signs or ataxia
  • Protecting their airway, GCS ≥ 13
  • Haemodynamically stable, lactate < 4 mmol/L
  • Concurrent alcohol withdrawal manageable on symptom-triggered therapy (CIWA-Ar < 15, no seizure history)
  • Needs 5+ days of IV thiamine, electrolyte repletion, nutrition and PT/OT
  • Unsafe to discharge for social reasons — no supervision, ongoing vomiting, cannot walk
  • GCS ≤ 8, or any failure to protect the airway
  • Coma, status epilepticus, or repeated seizures
  • Shock of any kind, or an unexplained lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L
  • Suspected wet or Shoshin beriberi — warm shock with a wide pulse pressure
  • Severe withdrawal: CIWA-Ar > 20, delirium tremens, or benzodiazepine requirements escalating despite protocol
  • Refeeding syndrome with phosphate < 1.0 mg/dL, arrhythmia, or respiratory failure
Admit under a diagnosis of "suspected Wernicke encephalopathy", not "alcohol intoxication" or "failure to thrive." The label determines whether the night team continues the thiamine. Auto-populated EMR order sets have been shown to significantly increase appropriate high-dose parenteral thiamine use — if your hospital does not have one, this is the single highest-yield quality-improvement project available to a resident.
Orders

Admission order set

🧪

What to order, in this order

Thiamine 500 mg IVFIRST ORDER, BEFORE ANY DEXTROSE. Three times daily. Dilute in 100 mL normal saline, infuse over 30 minutes.NOW
POC glucoseBefore you hang anything. If low, treat it immediately and push thiamine at the same time — do not hold the dextrose.NOW
Whole-blood thiamine (TDP)2 mL EDTA, protected from light, drawn before the first dose — only if the tube is already in your hand. Never delay the dose for the draw. Result takes 3–6 days and will not change management.If instant
Magnesium, phosphate, potassium, ionised calciumOn arrival, then at least daily — and every 6–12 h for the first 72 h once feeding starts. Hypomagnesemia causes thiamine-refractory Wernicke.NOW
Magnesium sulfate IVGive empirically alongside the first thiamine dose in any malnourished or alcohol-using patient; do not wait for the level to come back.NOW
CMP, CBC, LFTs, INR, albumin, lipase, CKAdmission baseline. Establishes liver disease (which decides your benzodiazepine), renal function, and the nutritional starting point.Admit
Lactate, VBGIf tachypnoeic, shocked, or with an unexplained anion gap. Thiamine deficiency is a genuine cause of type B lactic acidosis — a lactate that clears within hours of thiamine is nearly diagnostic.Admit
Ethanol level, urine drug screen, ammonia (if cirrhotic), TSH, B12, folate, zincAdmission. A negative ethanol in a heavy drinker predicts imminent withdrawal. 85% of patients with alcohol-associated hepatitis are zinc-deficient.Admit
HIV, hepatitis B and C serologies, RPRPer USPSTF screening in this population, and because AIDS accounts for 5% of non-alcoholic Wernicke.Admit
Non-contrast head CTTo exclude subdural haematoma or intracranial haemorrhage in a falling, coagulopathic patient. Not to diagnose Wernicke — CT sensitivity is 13%.If falls/focal
MRI brain with and without contrast (FLAIR, DWI)To support the diagnosis and exclude mimics — after the first thiamine dose, never before it. Write the clinical question on the requisition. Image early: signal can normalise within 2 days of treatment.Within 24–48 h
CIWA-Ar q1–4h + symptom-triggered benzodiazepine protocolIf any alcohol history. Wernicke and withdrawal coexist constantly.Admit
Folate 1 mg PO daily, multivitamin, thiamine-containing IV fluidsStandard co-repletion. Note that since US grain folic-acid fortification, true folate deficiency is now rare even in alcohol use disorder — give it, but do not attribute the encephalopathy to it.Admit
Nutrition consult + refeeding precautionsBefore the first tray. Start low-calorie and advance slowly; check electrolytes before and during. See the refeeding module below.Day 0
Bedside swallow screen ± SLPBefore any oral intake. Dysphagia from medullary involvement is under-recognised and is why these patients aspirate.Day 0
PT/OT, fall precautions, bed alarmDay 1. Ataxia plus neuropathy plus confusion is a fall waiting to happen — and it is the main driver of disposition.Day 1
Documented eye and gait examBefore the first dose and again at 6–12 h. Improvement in nystagmus or abduction is your diagnostic confirmation and your best prognostic sign.Serial
Social work / addiction medicine consultDay 1, not day of discharge. Pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorder should be started in hospital.Day 1
Do not order "banana bag." A standard banana bag contains 100 mg of thiamine — a prophylaxis dose. Ordering one for a patient with suspected Wernicke encephalopathy delivers one-fifteenth of the daily treatment dose while creating a chart entry that reads as though the patient was treated. It is the commonest way this diagnosis gets under-treated.
Treat

Thiamine — the full dose ladder

💊

Dose by indication, and how to step down

TREATING suspected or confirmed Wernicke encephalopathy
500 mg IV TID × ≥5 days→ continue until no further improvement→ 300 mg PO 2–3×/day→ 100 mg PO daily indefinitely

ASMBS Wernicke's Task Force 2025. Each dose diluted in 100 mL normal saline and infused over 30 minutes. Oral step-down continues at 300 mg two to three times daily until the risk factors resolve, then 100 mg daily indefinitely — the task force specifically warns that 100 mg orally straight after acute treatment "is likely inadequate in many patients," having observed a high rate of recurrent Wernicke after discharge.

RegimenStartContinue / titrateStep-down & maintenanceSource & when to pick it
Thiamine — treatment default 500 mg IV TID
(1500 mg/day)		 Minimum 5 days; keep going until there is no further improvement in signs and symptoms Then 300 mg PO 2–3×/day until risk factors resolve → 100 mg PO daily indefinitely ASMBS 2025 — the current, most explicit recommendation, and the one to use in the US. Restores TPP fast enough and at a high enough plasma gradient to cross the blood–brain barrier.
Thiamine — RCP regimen 500 mg IV every 8 h × 3 days Then 250 mg IV or IM daily × 3–5 days Then oral 50–100 mg daily Royal College of Physicians / UK practice. A defensible, slightly shorter alternative; ASMBS's ≥5 days of full dose is the more conservative choice.
Thiamine — EFNS regimen 200 mg IV three times daily Until no further improvement is observed Oral maintenance EFNS 2010. Lower than the ASMBS/RCP dose. Reasonable in a smaller patient or where supply is limited — but if you are choosing between them in a sick patient, choose the higher dose: thiamine's toxicity is essentially nil and under-dosing is the documented failure mode.
Thiamine — prophylaxis / treating deficiency without encephalopathy 100 mg IV or IM daily × 1–3 doses Continue until symptoms resolve and oral intake is adequate 100 mg PO daily ASMBS 2025 "secondary prevention." This is the banana-bag dose, and it is correct here — for the at-risk drinker in the ED with vomiting who has no neurological signs. It is not correct for suspected Wernicke.
Thiamine IM 250 mg IM daily × 3–5 days (high-risk prophylaxis) — — Use when there is genuinely no IV access. Practical ceiling: more than 100 mg IM daily is rarely tolerated because of injection-site pain — so IM cannot deliver a true treatment dose. Get a line.
Thiamine PO — rescue only Up to 1500 mg/day in divided doses — — Only when parenteral thiamine is unavailable. Above the saturable transporter, passive diffusion is not saturable, so 1500 mg PO does reach meaningful plasma levels. EFNS is nonetheless explicit that oral thiamine is ineffective for curing Wernicke — this is a stopgap, not a plan.
Magnesium sulfate mandatory partner 1–2 g IV or IM every 6–8 h while deficient Recheck serum magnesium daily; an alternative published regimen is 35–50 mmol of magnesium in 1 L of 0.9% saline infused over 12–24 h Magnesium oxide 400–800 mg PO daily once eating Mg²⁺ is required both by thiamine pyrophosphokinase (thiamine → TPP) and by transketolase itself. Without it your thiamine is inert. Reduce the dose and monitor closely in renal impairment — magnesium accumulates. (No Wernicke-specific guideline states a numeric magnesium target; a serum goal above 2.0 mg/dL is extrapolated general practice. The principle — check and replete, especially in non-responders — is guideline-supported.)
Folate1 mg PO daily—Continue through admission Routine co-repletion. Note that since US folic-acid grain fortification, true folate deficiency is now rare even in alcohol use disorder — give it, but do not let it explain the encephalopathy.
Multivitamin / B12 / zincMVI daily; B12 and zinc per level—Post-bariatric patients need lifelong bariatric-specific vitamins These are multi-deficiency patients. Zinc deficiency is present in 85% of alcohol-associated hepatitis and independently predicts 28-day mortality.
Why three times a day, and why so much? Free thiamine has a plasma half-life of about 96 minutes. A once-daily dose leaves the brain unexposed for most of the day, which is why every guideline divides it into two or three doses. And the dose is large because entry into brain at therapeutic concentrations depends on a steep plasma-to-brain gradient — 100 mg simply does not generate one.
The anaphylaxis fear is not a reason to withhold thiamine. ASMBS 2025 puts the risk at roughly 1 in 5 million administrations. The best primary data: in 1,070 consecutive 100 mg IV doses across 989 patients, there were adverse reactions in 1.1% and not a single case of anaphylaxis (Wrenn, Ann Emerg Med 1989); EFNS reports no significant adverse reactions in more than 300,000 treatments. Diluting in 100 mL of normal saline over 30 minutes reduces the side-effect risk further. Set that against a mortality of 5–20% and permanent amnesia in most untreated survivors. There is no rational version of this trade-off in which withholding wins.
Be honest about the evidence behind 500 mg TID — a resident should know this. The high-dose regimen is expert consensus, not trial-proven. A Cochrane review found the randomised evidence insufficient to guide dosing. Dingwall et al. (2022) randomised 520 patients across two trials to parenteral thiamine doses up to 500 mg three times daily and found no significant difference between any dose on cognition or neurological function — though the trials missed their enrolment targets, 44% of participants did not receive all study doses, and over 40% were lost to follow-up. A 2025 pharmacokinetic critique (Bonnan) goes further, arguing current protocols deliver roughly 7.8 times the whole-body store daily and proposing a single early 100 mg dose may suffice; no guideline has adopted it.

So why still give 500 mg TID? Because the argument is asymmetric, not superiority: thiamine has essentially no toxicity, the assay takes days, under-dosing is the documented failure mode across every case series, and the harm you are preventing — permanent amnesia — is irreversible. You are buying insurance with a drug that costs pennies. That is a defensible position, and it is a more honest one than claiming the dose is proven.
What if you do not know the prior dose, or the outside hospital's records are unavailable? Start at the full treatment dose — 500 mg IV TID. There is no accumulation risk and no titration to get wrong. Unlike almost every other drug in medicine, with thiamine the safe default when uncertain is more, sooner.
Co-treat

Concurrent alcohol withdrawal

🌡️

CIWA-Ar and why it must not distract you

Wernicke encephalopathy and alcohol withdrawal coexist constantly, and treating one does nothing for the other. Withdrawal is hyperadrenergic — tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, tremor, agitation, hallucinations, typically 48–96 hours after the last drink. Wernicke is hypoaroused, quiet and apathetic, with eye signs. Score the withdrawal, treat it on protocol, and keep the thiamine at full dose regardless of what the score does.

CIWA-Ar — Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol, revised

Ten items: nine scored 0–7, orientation scored 0–4. Maximum 67.

0
CIWA-Ar total (max 67)
Sullivan JT, Sykora K, Schneiderman J, Naranjo CA, Sellers EM. Assessment of alcohol withdrawal: the revised Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol scale (CIWA-Ar). Br J Addict 1989. Thresholds per MDCalc: medication generally begins at 8–10; scores above 20 prompt consideration of ICU transfer. CIWA-Ar requires a patient who can communicate — it is invalid in the intubated, severely encephalopathic, or non-verbal patient, which describes a great many Wernicke patients.
ASAM says not to use CIWA-Ar in a delirious patient — and that is most Wernicke patients. ASAM Recommendation VI.9, verbatim: "It is not recommended to use the CIWA-Ar in patients with delirium because it relies on patient-reported symptoms." Seven of the ten items require reliable self-report, so a confused or confabulating Wernicke–Korsakoff patient cannot be validly scored. Use CAM-ICU, RASS or a comparable observational tool instead. A CIWA-Ar of 3 in an obtunded patient means the instrument failed, not that the patient is well.
Benzodiazepine over-sedation reproduces the Wernicke triad exactly. ASAM lists its features as "ataxia, confusion, memory impairment, and delirium" — which is to say, the drug you gave for withdrawal produces the same four findings you are using to diagnose and follow Wernicke encephalopathy. Document the eye and mental-status exam before the first benzodiazepine dose, prefer symptom-triggered over fixed dosing, and when a patient fails to improve, ask whether you are looking at untreated Wernicke or at your own sedation.
Which benzodiazepine, and why. In significant liver disease choose lorazepam — it is cleared by glucuronidation and has no active metabolites, so it does not accumulate. Chlordiazepoxide and diazepam undergo hepatic oxidative metabolism and produce long-acting active metabolites, which is exactly what you do not want in a cirrhotic patient whose mental status you are trying to interpret. In a patient with normal liver function, the longer-acting agents give a smoother self-tapering course. ACG 2024 recommends cautious benzodiazepine use with careful monitoring as the treatment of choice in alcohol-associated liver disease with severe withdrawal. Confirm specific doses against your institution's withdrawal protocol — they vary substantially between hospitals, and the protocol you are working under is the one to follow.

PAWSS — Prediction of Alcohol Withdrawal Severity Scale

Use at admission to decide who needs prophylaxis and closer monitoring. Part A is a gate, not a scored item — if neither gate criterion is true, the patient is outside the withdrawal window and the tool does not apply.

A
Threshold gate
Any alcohol consumed within the last 30 days, OR a positive blood alcohol level on admission. If neither — stop, ask no further questions.
0
PAWSS score (max 10)
Maldonado JR, Sher Y, Ashouri JF, et al. Alcohol 2014;48:375–90 (development); prospective validation Maldonado JR, Sher Y, Das S, et al. Alcohol Alcohol 2015;50:509–18, n = 403 medicine and surgery inpatients: at a cutoff of ≥4, sensitivity 93.1% (95% CI 77.2–99.2) and specificity 99.5% (98.1–99.9), PPV 93.1%, NPV 99.5%, inter-rater concordance 0.963. Endorsed by ASAM (Recommendation VII.12) for predicting severe or complicated withdrawal in hospitalised medically ill patients. The >200 mg/dL blood-alcohol item is there because trauma patients presenting above that level had an odds ratio of 30.96 (19.5–49.2) for withdrawal.
Feed

Refeeding syndrome

🍽️

ASPEN 2020 — how to restart calories without causing harm

Every patient you are treating for Wernicke encephalopathy is, by definition, a refeeding-risk patient. And the mechanism overlaps exactly: restarting carbohydrate drives insulin, which pushes phosphate, potassium, magnesium and thiamine into cells. ASPEN's own table lists Wernicke's syndrome, Korsakoff psychosis and wet and dry beriberi as manifestations of the thiamine deficiency of severe refeeding syndrome.

ASPEN 2020 — thiamine in refeeding, verbatim

"Supplement thiamin 100 mg BEFORE feeding or before initiating dextrose-containing IV fluids in patients at risk." and "Supplement thiamin 100 mg/d for 5–7 days or longer in patients with severe starvation, chronic alcoholism, or other high risk for deficiency and/or signs of thiamin deficiency." ASPEN adds that "routine thiamin levels are unlikely to be of value."

Note the ceiling: 100 mg is a prophylaxis dose for a patient at risk. If you actually suspect Wernicke encephalopathy, the dose is 500 mg IV three times daily, not 100 mg.

Who is at risk — ASPEN 2020 adult criteria

ASPEN deliberately provides no "mild risk" tier for adults, "to do so would risk the creation of an oversensitive definition." Note the footnote that matters: electrolytes may be normal despite total-body deficiency.

CriterionModerate risk — need 2Significant risk — need 1
BMI16–18.5 kg/m²<16 kg/m²
Weight loss5% in 1 month7.5% in 3 months, or >10% in 6 months
Caloric intakeNone or negligible for 5–6 days; or <75% of estimated need for >7 days during acute illness; or <75% of need for >1 monthNone or negligible for >7 days; or <50% of need for >5 days during acute illness; or <50% of need for >1 month
Pre-feeding K / Phos / MgMinimally low, or normal now but recently needing single-dose supplementationModerately or significantly low, or recently needing significant or repeated supplementation
Body compositionModerate subcutaneous fat loss; mild-to-moderate muscle lossSevere fat and muscle loss

ASPEN's high-risk conditions list reads like the Wernicke risk list: chronic alcohol or drug use disorder, anorexia nervosa, hyperemesis gravidarum or protracted vomiting, post-bariatric surgery, malabsorptive states, cancer, AIDS, food insecurity and homelessness, prolonged fasting or hunger strike, advanced neurologic impairment, and dysphagia.

The restart plan

StepASPEN 2020 (US)NICE CG32 (UK)
Start at100–150 g of dextrose, or 10–20 kcal/kg, in the first 24 hours — counting enteral and parenteral glucose, including drugs infused in dextroseMaximum 10 kcal/kg/day; only 5 kcal/kg/day in extreme cases (BMI <14, or negligible intake >15 days) with continuous cardiac monitoring
Advance by33% of goal every 1–2 daysSlowly, to meet or exceed full needs by day 4–7
Thiamine100 mg before feeding, then 100 mg/day for 5–7 days or longer200–300 mg orally daily for the first 10 days, plus vitamin B co strong 1–2 tablets three times daily and a balanced multivitamin
ElectrolytesCheck K, Mg and Phos before starting; monitor every 12 hours for the first 3 days in high-risk patients. Replete per standards of care.Explicit targets: potassium 2–4 mmol/kg/day, phosphate 0.3–0.6 mmol/kg/day, magnesium 0.2 mmol/kg/day IV or 0.4 mmol/kg/day oral
If levels dropCut calories/dextrose by 50%, then re-advance by ~33% of goal every 1–2 days. Delay any increase in calories while phosphorus, potassium or magnesium are severely low.—
MonitoringVitals every 4 h for the first 24 h; cardiorespiratory monitoring if unstable or severely deficient; daily weights with intake/output; reassess daily until stable — defined as no electrolyte supplementation needed for 2 daysContinuous cardiac monitoring at 5 kcal/kg/day
The ASPEN severity definition is a percent drop, not an absolute number. Refeeding syndrome is defined as a fall in any one, two or three of serum phosphorus, potassium and/or magnesium by 10–20% (mild), 20–30% (moderate), or >30% and/or organ dysfunction (severe) — including organ dysfunction due to thiamine deficiency — occurring within 5 days of restarting or substantially increasing energy. So you need the baseline. Draw it before the first tray. ASPEN gives no absolute K/Phos/Mg cutoffs and explicitly defers repletion to local standards of care.
Monitor

Daily management & the recovery timeline

📈

What to trend, and what to expect

Trend dailyTarget / what a bad trend means
Eye exam — nystagmus, abduction, gazeThe most sensitive marker of response. Should begin improving within hours to days. No ocular improvement at 48–72 h means: check magnesium, confirm the thiamine is actually being given at the ordered dose, then question the diagnosis.
Gait — walked, not asked aboutDocument distance and assistive device. Drives PT/OT and disposition more than anything else in the chart.
Mental status / attentionImproves over days to weeks. Distinguish sedation from disease — if benzodiazepines are running, the confusion may be yours to fix.
Magnesium, phosphate, potassiumDaily, and q6–12 h for 72 h after feeding starts. Potassium will not correct until magnesium is corrected. A falling phosphate on day 2 of feeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise.
CIWA-Arq1–4h while withdrawal risk persists. Escalating requirements despite protocol is an ICU trigger.
Intake, weight, calorie countThe nutritional deficit is the disease. Weight and documented intake, not appetite reported on rounds.
Aspiration and fall eventsThe two things that actually kill these patients on the floor.

What recovers, and when — the conversation to have with the family

FeatureTimelineExtent of recovery
Ocular signs — nystagmus, ophthalmoplegiaHours to daysMost reversible feature. Ptosis and gaze palsies improve over days to weeks. This is your ex juvantibus confirmation.
Overall symptoms24–48 hoursSymptoms usually begin improving within 24–48 h of high-dose IV thiamine.
Confusion / apathyDays to weeksResponds well. As it clears, an underlying amnestic syndrome may be revealed that was invisible while the patient was globally confused.
AtaxiaAround the second week; weeks to monthsImproves in up to ~40%. Most patients are left with some residual gait disturbance — plan rehab, not cure.
Memory / KorsakoffOften permanentPoor recovery. Thiamine prevents progression far more reliably than it reverses established deficits. Do not promise recovery — but note there are reports of substantial late improvement with sustained high-dose therapy, so do not write patients off either.
Peripheral neuropathyMonthsSlow axonal regrowth; improves with sustained repletion and abstinence.
Do not stop at day 5 because the eyes look better. ASMBS says to continue high-dose IV thiamine "until no further improvement" — the ocular signs recover first and fastest, so eye recovery marks the beginning of treatment, not the end. Stopping when the nystagmus clears is how a reversible Wernicke becomes a permanent Korsakoff.
Escalate

When to call the ICU

⬆️

Numeric escalation triggers

TriggerThresholdWhy
Airway / consciousnessGCS ≤ 8, or a falling GCS, or inability to clear secretionsComa occurs in <5% of Wernicke but carries the highest mortality; aspiration in a dysphagic, ataxic, confused patient is the commonest terminal event on a ward.
SeizuresAny second seizure, or status epilepticusMore common in non-alcoholic Wernicke with cortical involvement; also withdrawal seizures.
HaemodynamicsMAP < 65 mmHg despite fluids, or any vasopressor requirementConsider Shoshin beriberi — warm shock with a wide pulse pressure in a malnourished patient responds to thiamine, not to escalating noradrenaline.
Lactate≥ 4 mmol/L, or rising despite resuscitationType B lactic acidosis from pyruvate dehydrogenase blockade — or sepsis. Either way, unit-level care.
WithdrawalCIWA-Ar > 20, delirium tremens, or escalating benzodiazepine requirements despite a symptom-triggered protocolNeeds continuous monitoring and often phenobarbital or dexmedetomidine.
RefeedingPhosphate < 1.0 mg/dL, or any arrhythmia, or respiratory muscle weaknessSevere hypophosphataemia causes its own encephalopathy, haemolysis and respiratory failure.
RespiratoryNew hypoxaemia, aspiration event, or rising work of breathingAspiration pneumonitis in a dysphagic patient.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness and where they go

Discharge readiness — all of the following:

  • Completed at least 5 days of high-dose IV thiamine and no further day-to-day improvement in signs
  • Tolerating oral intake, with a documented safe swallow
  • Magnesium, potassium and phosphate stable for 48 h off IV repletion
  • Out of the withdrawal window with a stable CIWA-Ar off benzodiazepines for 24 h
  • Mobilising safely at whatever level PT has established, with equipment in place
  • Oral thiamine 300 mg 2–3×/day dispensed in hand, with an explicit stop/step-down plan, plus MVI and any other repletion
  • Alcohol use disorder pharmacotherapy started (not "offered at follow-up") and a follow-up appointment booked
  • A realistic assessment of who is supervising this person, and whether they have decision-making capacity

Home

Full recovery of gait and cognition, reliable supervision, and able to self-administer medications. A minority of these patients.

Home health

Mild residual ataxia or neuropathy; nursing for medication management plus home PT. Needs someone at home who can supervise.

SNF

Needs 24-hour skilled nursing but tolerates less than 3 h of therapy per day — the common destination for a deconditioned patient with residual ataxia.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h of therapy daily across ≥2 disciplines and has clear rehab potential. Best for isolated ataxia and neuropathy with preserved cognition.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care — ventilator weaning, tracheostomy, multi-organ recovery after an ICU course.

Supervised / memory care

Established Korsakoff syndrome. Dense anterograde amnesia means the patient cannot reliably take medication, keep appointments, or manage risk — regardless of how well they converse. Formal capacity assessment and often guardianship.
Capacity in Korsakoff syndrome is the most commonly botched judgement on this disease. These patients have preserved language, attention span, social manner and procedural memory. They interview beautifully. They will agree to every discharge instruction, and they will not remember any of it. Assess capacity by testing recall of the plan after a delay, not by whether the conversation went well. Corroborate the history and the plan with a family member. And be careful with driving: an amnestic patient with residual ataxia and neuropathy should not be driving, and someone has to say so explicitly.
Rehabilitation is not futile in Korsakoff syndrome, it is just different. Errorless learning — teaching a task in a way that prevents mistakes from being encoded — has repeatedly been shown to help patients relearn instrumental activities such as making a pot of coffee, improving autonomy and independent living. Physical rehabilitation improves strength, ambulation and self-care. Refer rather than write off. Also plan for behaviour: aggression is described in 20–54% of Korsakoff patients, depression in about 18%, psychotic symptoms in 7%.
Readmission is the norm, so plan for it. One-year readmission is 31.6% after alcohol-related Wernicke versus 18.7% after non-alcohol-related. The ASMBS task force reports a high incidence of recurrent Wernicke after discharge, which is precisely why they raised the post-discharge oral dose to 300 mg two or three times daily and advise frequent in-person reassessment. A discharge with 100 mg daily and no follow-up is a booked readmission.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

When Wernicke belongs in the unit

Thiamine deficiency is an ICU disease that nobody codes as one. Between 30% and 90% of critically ill patients are thiamine-deficient, and up to 70% of those admitted with septic shock. In acute critical illness with no intake, deficiency can develop within 72 hours — far faster than the 2–3 weeks it takes in an ambulatory patient, because fever and sepsis raise the requirement while intake is zero and renal and dialytic losses continue.
ICU triggerThreshold
Airway / neurologicGCS ≤ 8, falling GCS, inability to protect the airway or clear secretions, coma (<5% of Wernicke but the highest-mortality subgroup)
Status epilepticusAny seizure >5 min, or two seizures without return to baseline. More common in non-alcoholic Wernicke with cortical involvement, and in withdrawal.
ShockMAP <65 mmHg after adequate fluid, or any vasopressor requirement — and specifically, warm vasodilated shock in a malnourished patient, which is Shoshin beriberi until disproven
Lactate≥4 mmol/L, or rising despite resuscitation, or an unexplained type B lactic acidosis
Severe withdrawalCIWA-Ar >20, delirium tremens, withdrawal seizures, or benzodiazepine requirements escalating despite a symptom-triggered protocol
Severe refeeding syndromePhosphate <1.0 mg/dL, arrhythmia, haemolysis, or respiratory muscle weakness after feeding is restarted
Respiratory failureAspiration event with hypoxaemia, or rising work of breathing in a dysphagic ataxic patient
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

ItemDetail
Central accessFor vasopressors, concentrated electrolytes and reliable thiamine delivery. Do not let line placement delay the first thiamine dose — give it peripherally.
Arterial lineIf on vasopressors or with a severe acidosis. In beriberi shock it also lets you see the wide pulse pressure of a vasodilated, high-output state.
Cardiac output assessmentEcho, or a device that gives cardiac index and SVR. This is the study that distinguishes high-output beriberi shock from cardiogenic shock — the ventricle is hyperdynamic, not failing.
Lactateq2–4h during resuscitation. A lactate that falls sharply within hours of thiamine, without any other change, is close to diagnostic of thiamine deficiency.
Magnesium, phosphate, potassium, ionised calciumq6–12h for the first 72 h of feeding, then daily. Potassium will not correct until magnesium is corrected.
Continuous EEGIf unexplained persistent coma or fluctuating consciousness after 24–48 h of full-dose thiamine — non-convulsive status is the mimic you cannot see.
Serial neuro exam including eyesDocument nystagmus, abduction and pupils every shift. In a sedated patient this is the only response signal you have, so protect it: use the lightest effective sedation.
Daily gait/mobility once ableEarly mobility is both treatment and assessment.
Sedation erases your only bedside marker. Benzodiazepines, propofol and opioids all blunt the mental status and eye findings you are using to track response. Where possible, get the neurological exam documented before sedation starts, and use daily interruption or a dexmedetomidine-based strategy so you retain something to follow.
Recognise

Shoshin beriberi — the shock that thiamine reverses

💔

Warm shock in a malnourished patient

Shoshin beriberi is fulminant, decompensated cardiac beriberi: shock with a markedly elevated lactate and metabolic acidosis, often with abdominal pain and anorexia, and sometimes hypothermia. It is a great imitator — the haemodynamics look like septic shock, so patients receive fluid, antibiotics and escalating noradrenaline while the actual deficit is a vitamin. The FDA label for thiamine hydrochloride injection explicitly names "cardiovascular disease due to thiamine deficiency" and "infantile beriberi with acute collapse" among the situations requiring rapid parenteral restoration.

FeatureShoshin / wet beriberiSeptic shockCardiogenic shock
Cardiac outputHigh — hyperdynamic ventricleHigh (usually)Low
SVRLow — profound peripheral vasodilationLowHigh (compensatory)
Pulse pressureWideWideNarrow
ExtremitiesWarmWarmCold, mottled
LactateVery high, often out of proportion to perfusion — type B, from pyruvate dehydrogenase blockadeHigh, from hypoperfusionHigh, from hypoperfusion
Venous congestionRaised CVP, peripheral oedema, sometimes pulmonary hypertensionVariableRaised filling pressures
Infectious sourceNonePresentNone
Nutritional contextAlways — alcohol, post-bariatric, prolonged vomiting, starvation, TPN without vitaminsMay coexistMay coexist
Response to IV thiamineDramatic, within hours — lactate falls, pressor requirement dropsNoneNone
The diagnostic move is simply to give the thiamine. In a malnourished patient with warm shock, a wide pulse pressure and a lactate that does not fit the perfusion state, give thiamine 500 mg IV and watch the lactate and the noradrenaline requirement over the next few hours. You lose nothing if you are wrong. If you are right, you have found the one form of shock that is corrected by a vitamin — and pressors, which do not address the metabolic block, are a much less effective treatment for it.
There is also a gastrointestinal beriberi: abdominal pain, anorexia, nausea and vomiting, gastroparesis and ileus with an alarmingly high lactate. It is repeatedly worked up as an acute abdomen, and untreated it commonly progresses to Wernicke encephalopathy — while the vomiting deepens the very deficiency that caused it. Unexplained abdominal pain with a high lactate and a normal CT in a malnourished patient deserves a dose of thiamine.
Wet beriberi with generalised oedema and the "air hunger" facies of high-output failure. Photographed on admission, one week before death from heart failure — a reminder of what the untreated natural history looks like.

Support

Pressors & haemodynamic support

💉

Which drip — while the thiamine works

Doses are the standard vasoactive ranges used across this reference set (Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 for the sepsis indications). In beriberi shock these are a bridge, not the treatment.

AgentReceptors / mechanismStart → titrate → ceilingEffectWhen to pick it here
Norepinephrineα1 ≫ β1~0.05 mcg/kg/min → titrate q5–10 min → practical ceiling ~0.5↑↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line for the vasodilated shock of beriberi and for any coexisting septic shock. Counteracts the low SVR while thiamine restores oxidative metabolism.
VasopressinV1 receptor — non-catecholamine0.03 U/min fixed — do not titrate↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingSecond agent, added when norepinephrine reaches ~0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min. Useful in acidosis, where catecholamine receptors respond poorly.
Epinephrineα + β1 + β2~0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min → titrate → ~0.5+↑CO + ↑SVRThird-line. Caveat specific to this disease: epinephrine drives glycolysis and independently raises lactate, so it will muddy the one number you are using to track the thiamine response.
Angiotensin IIAT1 receptorStart 20 ng/kg/min per label, titrate↑SVRCatecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock.
Dobutamineβ1 > β2 (inotrope)2.5 mcg/kg/min → titrate → 20 mcg/kg/min↑CO, may ↓SVROnly if the echo shows genuinely low output. In classic wet beriberi the output is already high, so adding an inotrope worsens the vasodilation without helping.
Vasopressors raise blood pressure by constricting vessels; they do nothing about a cell that cannot make ATP. That is why the response in beriberi shock is disappointing until thiamine goes in — and why an unexpectedly pressor-refractory vasodilated shock in a malnourished patient should trigger a dose of thiamine rather than a fourth agent.
Evidence

Thiamine in sepsis — what the trials actually showed

📊

The metabolic cocktail question, answered honestly

Bottom line You are not giving thiamine for sepsis. You are giving it because deficiency is present in a large majority of critically ill patients, the assay takes days, and the drug is essentially non-toxic. That is a nutritional-repletion indication, not a metabolic-resuscitation one — and the distinction is worth teaching explicitly, because conflating the two is how residents end up either ordering a discredited cocktail or withholding a vitamin.
QuestionThe evidenceWhat to do
Should I give the "metabolic cocktail" (vitamin C + thiamine + hydrocortisone)? No. The 2017 before-and-after study that started this reported 8.5% versus 40.4% mortality, but it was retrospective, single-centre, n = 94, with historical controls. Every subsequent randomised trial missed its primary endpoint: VITAMINS (2020, n = 211) — vasopressor-free time 122.1 vs 124.6 h, p = 0.83; VICTAS (2021, n = 501) — ventilator- and vasopressor-free days 25 vs 26, p = 0.85; ACTS (2020, n = 200) — SOFA change difference −0.8 (95% CI −1.7 to 0.2), p = 0.12. A meta-analysis of 9 RCTs and 1,427 patients found hospital mortality RR 1.07 (0.85–1.34) and reached its required information size. Component analyses attribute the small SOFA and vasopressor signal to the steroid, not the vitamins. Do not order it.
Is high-dose IV vitamin C at least harmless? No — it caused harm. LOVIT (2022, n = 863): death or persistent organ dysfunction at day 28 in 44.5% versus 38.5%, RR 1.21 (95% CI 1.04–1.40), p = 0.01, with one life-threatening anaphylaxis in the vitamin C arm. Both Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 and 2026 suggest against using IV vitamin C in sepsis or septic shock. Actively avoid.
Does thiamine improve outcomes in undifferentiated septic shock? Not demonstrated. Donnino (2016, n = 88, thiamine 200 mg IV BID × 7 d) missed its primary endpoint — 24-hour lactate 2.5 vs 2.6 mmol/L, p = 0.40. TRPSS (2023, n = 88) missed its primary renal endpoint, p = 0.07. A 2026 meta-analysis of 9 studies and 520 patients found no short-term mortality benefit (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.54–1.12). Neither SSC 2021 nor SSC 2026 contains any adult thiamine recommendation, and the 2026 paediatric companion suggests against it. Do not give it as a sepsis therapy.
Does it help the patient who is actually deficient? The signal is consistent in every deficiency-stratified analysis — though all of it is hypothesis-generating. Donnino's pre-specified thiamine-deficient subgroup (35% of the trial) had lower lactate (p = 0.03) and a mortality difference over time (p = 0.047). The 2026 meta-analysis found OR 0.18 (0.05–0.69) for mortality in deficient patients. A pooled patient-level post-hoc reported adjusted OR 8.17 (1.79–37.22) for being alive and dialysis-free. Tellingly, TRPSS explicitly excluded anyone with a clinical indication for thiamine — that is, the very patients most likely to benefit. Treat the deficiency.
The guideline that does tell you to give it — ESPEN 2024 practical short micronutrient guideline

Recommendation 14.5 (Grade B, 80% consensus): "In patients admitted to emergency or intensive care, the administration of thiamine (100–300 mg/day IV) should be prescribed without hesitation from admission for 3–4 days."

Recommendation 14.6 (Grade B, 92% consensus): for ward admissions with any suspicion of reduced food intake in preceding days, or high alcohol consumption — thiamine 100–300 mg/day orally or IV.

ESPEN notes that deficiency or depletion "may be found in over 90% of [critically ill] patients," that the IV route is most efficient at 3 × 100–300 mg/day, and — the line worth remembering — "No toxicity. The only effect of high doses is increased urinary excretion." This, not a sepsis trial, is the citation to quote when someone asks why you are giving thiamine to an ICU admission.

Two adjacent situations worth knowing. In metformin-associated lactic acidosis there are zero trials of thiamine; standard care is supportive with extracorporeal removal per EXTRIP (dialysis when lactate >20 mmol/L or pH ≤7.0, continued until lactate <3 and pH >7.35). The rationale for adding thiamine is a hypothesis — metformin and thiamine compete for the same transporters — plus a couple of striking single cases. It is a defensible zero-risk adjunct, not a treatment. In refractory vasoplegia, empiric IV thiamine belongs on the checklist alongside hydrocortisone, methylene blue and hydroxocobalamin: cheap, non-toxic, and occasionally curative when the cause turns out to be beriberi. There is no randomised evidence for either use — say so.
Airway

Airway & ventilation

🌬️

Why these patients get intubated

Wernicke encephalopathy itself rarely causes respiratory failure. These patients are intubated for airway protection in coma or status epilepticus, and for aspiration — the combination of medullary dysphagia, ataxia and confusion. Add severe hypophosphataemia from refeeding, which weakens the diaphragm, and the pattern is complete.
