Watch the phosphate before you plan extubation. Severe hypophosphataemia from refeeding causes diaphragmatic weakness and is a classic cause of a failed spontaneous breathing trial in exactly this population. Check it, correct it, then re-test.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

DomainReady to move
AirwayExtubated ≥12–24 h with protected airway, secretions manageable, swallow screened
HaemodynamicsOff all vasopressors ≥12–24 h with MAP >65 mmHg
LactateCleared to <2 mmol/L and stable
NeurologicGCS ≥13, no seizure for ≥24 h on a stable regimen
WithdrawalCIWA-Ar <10 on a stable or falling benzodiazepine requirement, off any infusion ≥12–24 h
ElectrolytesPhosphate >2.0 mg/dL, magnesium and potassium stable for 24 h on maintenance repletion
ThiamineContinuing 500 mg IV TID — the downgrade does not change the dose. Write it explicitly in the transfer note.
Not yet if… the lactate is still falling but not normal; the phosphate is still dropping with each feed advance; the benzodiazepine requirement is stable only because an infusion is running; the patient has had an aspiration event within 24 h; or — the one most often overlooked — the thiamine dose is about to be quietly reduced on transfer. Under-dosing at handoff is the single commonest failure in this disease. State the dose, the route, the frequency and the intended duration in the transfer note, and say explicitly that it continues until there is no further improvement.
If the patient survives to downgrade with residual amnesia, the ICU is where the goals-of-care conversation should start, not where it should be deferred. Established Korsakoff syndrome carries a median survival of about 10.7 years — considerably better than alcohol-related dementia at 5.9 years, so this is a conversation about long-term supervised living and continued abstinence, not about end of life.
Shared

Comorbidity interactions

🔗

How each comorbidity changes the course — and your management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseHow it changes your management
Cirrhosis / hepatic encephalopathy The single commonest reason Wernicke is missed — the confusion gets attributed to ammonia and the eyes are never examined. It also degrades the Caine criteria, whose sensitivity approaches 100% only in alcoholic patients without hepatic encephalopathy. Impaired hepatic phosphorylation of thiamine to TPP compounds the deficiency. Treat both, always. A raised ammonia does not exclude Wernicke, and a normal one does not exclude hepatic encephalopathy. Lactulose plus full-dose IV thiamine. Choose lorazepam for withdrawal (glucuronidated, no active metabolites) rather than chlordiazepoxide or diazepam, which accumulate in liver failure.
Alcohol withdrawal Coexists constantly. Withdrawal is hyperadrenergic and agitated; Wernicke is hypoaroused and apathetic with eye signs. Each masks the other. Run a symptom-triggered protocol and full-dose thiamine simultaneously. Remember that the benzodiazepines you give will sedate the patient and erase the mental-status and ocular exam you were using to track the thiamine response — document the exam before you start dosing.
CKD / dialysis Thiamine is small and water-soluble, so it is dialysed off — plasma levels fall by about 50% in some haemodialysis patients. In one report of nine dialysis-dependent Wernicke cases, seven were diagnosed post-mortem. Give thiamine after the dialysis session, not before. Continue daily oral thiamine as part of a renal vitamin. Reduce magnesium repletion and monitor closely — magnesium accumulates in renal failure, so the usual aggressive repletion becomes dangerous.
Heart failure Bidirectional: thiamine deficiency causes high-output failure (wet beriberi), and heart failure is itself a risk factor for deficiency. One study found 300 mg/day orally for 28 days improved LVEF by 30%. If the echo shows a hyperdynamic ventricle with low SVR in a malnourished patient, stop treating it as cardiogenic and give thiamine. Loop diuretics have long been suspected of increasing urinary thiamine loss — the evidence is genuinely mixed, so supplement rather than withhold diuresis.
Diabetes mellitus Thiamine levels run 50–75% lower than in people without diabetes, probably from increased renal clearance, and worsen with albuminuria. Every hypoglycaemia correction and every dextrose infusion is a thiamine stressor. Metformin reduces the ThTR-2 intestinal transporter, compounding it. Supplement, and give thiamine with dextrose.
Pregnancy / hyperemesis gravidarum Accounts for 12.2% of non-alcoholic Wernicke. Fetal loss in 50% and maternal death in 5% of a 177-case series — with subtherapeutic dosing in two-thirds. Thiamine before every dextrose-containing fluid and before every dose of parenteral nutrition. Do not reduce the dose out of caution about pregnancy: under-dosing is the documented harm here, not over-dosing.
Bariatric surgery 29% deficient pre-operatively, 25% post-operatively; 79–94% of post-bariatric Wernicke presents within 6 months. Malabsorptive operations carry higher risk than restrictive ones. Lifelong bariatric-specific vitamins with at least 12 mg/day of thiamine. Persistent vomiting means parenteral repletion, not a stronger tablet. Follow levels for 6 months post-op.
Malignancy & chemotherapy Cancer is the single largest non-alcoholic category (18.1%). Thiamine deficiency in 55% of hospitalised oncology patients, 80% of whom had a mental status abnormality. Suspect it in any oncology patient with new confusion before you settle on metastases, delirium, or opioids. 5-fluorouracil and ifosfamide are specific culprits (below).
Sepsis / critical illness 30–90% of critically ill patients and up to 70% of ICU septic shock admissions are thiamine-deficient. Deficiency can develop within 72 hours. Treat the deficiency; do not adopt the vitamin C + thiamine + steroid "metabolic cocktail" as protocol. Shoshin beriberi mimics septic shock — in warm shock with a lactate that does not fit, give thiamine.
Anorexia nervosa & restrictive eating Thiamine deficiency in about 38% of patients with anorexia nervosa; the highest mortality of any psychiatric disorder. Thiamine before the first calories, then refeeding precautions with daily electrolytes. Psychiatric labels are why these patients get their neurological signs dismissed.
Psychiatric illness generally In 262 psychiatric inpatients, Caine-positive Wernicke–Korsakoff prevalence was 12%, and only half used alcohol. In schizophrenia, reported Wernicke cases mostly present with the full triad — because the earlier stages were dismissed as psychiatric. Examine the eyes and walk the patient. Aggression is described in 20–54% of Korsakoff patients, depression in 18%, psychotic symptoms in 7% — behaviour that is easily mistaken for primary psychiatric illness.
Thyroid disease Thyrotoxicosis raises thiamine requirement and accounts for 1.3% of non-alcoholic Wernicke; hypothyroidism independently causes cognitive slowing and mimics the picture. Check TSH in any atypical presentation. Treating the thyroid disease without repleting thiamine leaves the deficiency in place.
Refeeding / hypophosphataemia Refeeding consumes thiamine, phosphate, potassium and magnesium simultaneously. Severe hypophosphataemia causes its own encephalopathy, haemolysis and respiratory muscle weakness. Thiamine before calories. Advance feeds slowly with electrolytes checked before and during. A falling phosphate on day 2 of feeding is refeeding syndrome until proven otherwise — and it is a common cause of a failed extubation.
HIV / AIDS 5.0% of published non-alcoholic Wernicke cases. Screen per USPSTF. HIV encephalopathy and CNS opportunistic infection are simultaneous mimics — treat thiamine empirically while working them up.
Drugs to avoid or use with real caution
Drug / interventionMechanism of harmWhat to do instead
IV dextrose before thiamineDrives glycolysis and consumes the last remaining TPP at pyruvate dehydrogenase, precipitating or worsening Wernicke. In thiamine-depleted animals a glucose infusion caused thalamic acidosis and blood–brain barrier disruption within 40 minutes.Thiamine first, or simultaneously. But never withhold glucose from a hypoglycaemic patient — treat the sugar and push thiamine in the same breath.
MetronidazoleActs as a thiamine analogue and inhibits thiamine absorption, producing a functional deficiency even when the measured thiamine level is normal. It also causes its own encephalopathy — dysarthria, gait instability, limb dyscoordination — with MRI lesions in the dentate nuclei (~90%) and splenium.Stop the drug if the picture fits, and give thiamine anyway: the pathophysiology overlaps.
Metformin and other ThTR-2 inhibitors — verapamil, quinapril, amitriptyline, sertraline, amoxapine, penicillamine, quinidine, trimethoprim, hydroxychloroquineReduce the intestinal ThTR-2 thiamine transporter, worsening an already saturable and inefficient absorption pathway.You do not usually need to stop them — but recognise that oral thiamine will work even less well in these patients, and lower your threshold for parenteral repletion.
5-fluorouracilIts metabolite blocks the Krebs cycle and interferes with thiamine phosphate formation — a chemical version of the same lesion.Supplement thiamine proactively; suspect it early in a 5-FU patient with new confusion.
IfosfamideCauses a Wernicke-like encephalopathy.Consider thiamine, and consider methylene blue per your oncology protocol for ifosfamide neurotoxicity.
Loop diuretics (furosemide)Long thought to increase urinary thiamine loss — but a study of 73 patients over 65 found no association. Genuinely contested.Do not withhold needed diuresis. Supplement thiamine and say "possible," not "established," when you teach it.
Benzodiazepines and other sedativesDo not worsen Wernicke, but they erase the mental-status and ocular exam you are using to track the response — and they make an under-treated Wernicke look like adequate withdrawal control.Document the neurological exam before sedation. Use symptom-triggered rather than fixed dosing, and prefer the lightest effective regimen.
"Banana bag" as treatmentContains 100 mg of thiamine — one-fifteenth of the daily treatment dose — while generating a chart entry that reads as though the patient was treated.Correct for prophylaxis in an at-risk patient without neurological signs. Never for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy.
Parenteral nutrition without multivitaminsCauses frank thiamine deficiency in days to weeks; historic US multivitamin-infusion shortages caused fatal Wernicke encephalopathy.Verify that the multivitamin is actually in the bag — this is a recurring, checkable supply-chain hazard.
Shared

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The things that actually change what you do

  1. The triad is the exception, not the rule. Complete in 10–20%; 19% of autopsy-proven cases had no documented signs. Use the Caine criteria — two of four, ~85% sensitive — not the triad.
  2. Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis and treatment is the diagnostic test. Whole-blood thiamine takes 3–6 days and can be normal; MRI misses about half. Treat and watch the eyes.
  3. A normal MRI does not exclude it. Sensitivity 53%. And acute signal change can normalise within two days of thiamine, so a late scan is negative for the best possible reason.
  4. Hypomagnesemia causes thiamine-refractory Wernicke. Magnesium is required both to convert thiamine to TPP and by transketolase itself. The patient "not responding to thiamine" very often has a magnesium of 1.2. Check it and replete it.
  5. Banana bags contain 100 mg of thiamine — a prophylaxis dose. Treating suspected Wernicke needs 500 mg IV three times daily. The banana bag is the commonest way this disease gets under-treated while looking treated in the chart.
  6. Oral thiamine cannot treat this. A 20 mg oral dose delivers ~4.8 mg to a healthy person and ~1.5 mg to someone who drinks; bioavailability is 3.7–5.3%. EFNS: oral thiamine "is ineffective in… curing WE."
  7. Give thiamine before or with glucose — but never delay glucose for hypoglycaemia. The systematic review found no evidence above case-report level that a single ampoule of D50 causes harm. Treat the sugar; push the thiamine at the same time.
  8. Divide the dose. Free thiamine has a plasma half-life of about 96 minutes, which is why every guideline gives it two or three times daily rather than once.
  9. Anaphylaxis is roughly 1 in 5 million. The fear of it is not a reason to withhold a vitamin from a patient facing 5–20% mortality and an 85% rate of permanent amnesia. Dilute in 100 mL of saline over 30 minutes and give it.
  10. Ocular signs recover in hours; memory often does not. Improvement in nystagmus or abduction confirms the diagnosis — but it marks the start of treatment, not the end. Continue high-dose IV thiamine until there is no further improvement.
  11. You must walk the patient. Ataxia is documented in only 23% of cases largely because observing gait is omitted from the neurological exam — and it is often the earliest sign, preceding the others by days to weeks.
  12. Hold lateral gaze for ten full seconds. Gaze-evoked nystagmus is the most common ocular finding and a one-second glance will miss it.
  13. Half of all cases are not alcohol-related, and those are the ones you will miss. Only 6–16% of non-alcoholic cases are diagnosed antemortem, and their in-hospital mortality is higher (8.5% vs 3.2%) precisely because of the delay.
  14. In non-alcoholic Wernicke, "atypical" MRI is the expected pattern. Cerebellum, dentate, cranial nerve nuclei, splenium, cortex. Do not let an atypical read talk you out of the diagnosis.
  15. Hepatic encephalopathy is the commonest reason Wernicke is missed — and it degrades the Caine criteria exactly where you most need them. When both are plausible, treat both.
  16. Persistent vomiting after bariatric surgery is the trigger. Most post-bariatric Wernicke presents within 3–4 months; nausea and vomiting are both cause and effect, so it becomes a vicious cycle — often with no anatomic complication at all.
  17. Warm shock plus a lactate that does not fit the perfusion state, in a malnourished patient, is Shoshin beriberi until disproven. Give 500 mg of IV thiamine and watch the lactate and the pressor requirement.
  18. Discharging on 100 mg of oral thiamine daily is under-treating. ASMBS raised the post-discharge dose to 300 mg two to three times daily until risk factors resolve, after observing a high rate of recurrent Wernicke — and one-year readmission is 31.6% after alcohol-related cases.
  19. Korsakoff patients interview beautifully and remember nothing. Assess capacity by testing recall of the plan after a delay, not by how the conversation went. Corroborate with family. Address driving explicitly.
  20. Rehabilitation is not futile in Korsakoff syndrome. Errorless learning helps patients relearn instrumental activities and improves independence. Refer rather than write off.
  21. Build the order set. Auto-populated EMR order sets significantly increase appropriate use of high-dose parenteral thiamine. In a disease whose entire failure mode is under-recognition and under-dosing, that is the intervention with the largest population effect.
  22. When in doubt, treat. Thiamine costs pennies, has essentially no toxicity, and the downside of unnecessary treatment is nothing. The downside of missing it is a person who will never form a new memory again.

High-dose vitamin C is not a harmless add-on.
ASPEN Refeeding Consensus
Nutr Clin Pract 35:178–95		2020 Consensus recommendations for identifying and managing refeeding syndrome in adults and children Risk stratification into moderate and significant tiers; caloric restart at 10–20 kcal/kg/day advancing 33% of goal every 1–2 days; severity defined as a 10–20% / 20–30% / >30% fall in phosphorus, potassium or magnesium within 5 days; thiamine 100 mg before feeding The protocol that governs the first tray in every Wernicke patient. Its own table lists Wernicke's syndrome and Korsakoff psychosis as manifestations of refeeding thiamine deficiency.
ESPEN practical short micronutrient guideline
Clin Nutr 43:825–57		2024 European consensus guideline on micronutrients Rec 14.5 (Grade B): thiamine 100–300 mg/day IV from admission for 3–4 days in every emergency or intensive care admission, "without hesitation." Rec 14.6 (Grade B): the same dose for ward admissions with reduced intake or high alcohol use The citation to use when someone asks why you are giving thiamine to an ICU patient — a nutritional-repletion indication rather than a sepsis one, and the only guideline that states it plainly.
Maldonado et al. (PAWSS)
Alcohol Alcohol 50:509–18		2015 Prospective validation, n = 403 medicine and surgery inpatients At a cutoff of ≥4: sensitivity 93.1%, specificity 99.5%, PPV 93.1%, NPV 99.5%, inter-rater concordance 0.963 Lets you identify, on admission, who will develop complicated withdrawal — endorsed by ASAM for hospitalised medically ill patients.
Bush et al. (AUDIT-C)
Arch Intern Med 158:1789		1998 Validation in 243 male VA general-medicine patients At ≥4: sensitivity 86%, specificity 72% for heavy drinking and/or active abuse or dependence (+LR 3.07). At ≥3: identifies 90% with abuse/dependence but specificity falls to 60% The three-question screen behind the USPSTF Grade B recommendation. Note the cohort was predominantly white male veterans with a mean age of 67.
ASMBS Wernicke's Task Force
Surg Obes Relat Dis		2025 Systematic literature review (2013–present) with expert consensus recommendations Treat Wernicke with 500 mg IV TID for at least 5 days, continuing until no further improvement; step down to 300 mg PO 2–3×/day, then 100 mg daily indefinitely; replace magnesium, potassium and phosphate; anaphylaxis ~1 in 5 million The current standard of care and the primary source for the dosing in this guide. Notably reframes Wernicke prophylaxis as analogous to VTE prophylaxis — a routine, protocolised preventive act.

What changed recently — the 2024–2026 era

DevelopmentDateWhat it means for you
ASMBS Wernicke's Task Force guidelines2025The first Wernicke-specific society guideline since EFNS 2010. Introduces a three-tier prevention framework with explicit doses, extends prophylaxis to GLP-1 medical weight loss, mandates magnesium, potassium and phosphate replacement, and states: "Wernicke's is an emergency. Draw labs and treat simultaneously." This is now the primary dosing reference in the US.
ESPEN practical short micronutrient guideline2024Gives the ICU/ED thiamine recommendation that Surviving Sepsis never has: 100–300 mg/day IV from admission for 3–4 days, Grade B, noting deficiency or depletion in over 90% of critically ill patients and "no toxicity."
ACG guideline on alcohol-associated liver diseaseJan 2024Key Concept 25: thiamine, B12 and zinc deficiencies are common in alcohol-associated hepatitis and should be supplemented, with thiamine helping prevent Wernicke. Gives baclofen a strong recommendation for alcohol use disorder in compensated liver disease.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026Mar 2026129 statements. Continues to suggest against IV vitamin C and still contains no adult thiamine recommendation. The paediatric companion suggests against thiamine in children with sepsis, while noting benefit may exist in documented deficiency.
⚠️ UK Pabrinex shortageAug 2024 →IV Pabrinex out of stock since August 2024; the intramuscular preparation has been discontinued. Unlicensed imports are being sourced, with interim dosing of 200–300 mg once daily for prophylaxis and 300–500 mg three times daily for treatment. Oral 50 mg and 100 mg tablets remain available. If you practise in the UK, check supply before you write the order.
⚠️ Parenteral multivitamin shortages cause Wernicke — again2022–23During an eight-month US shortage, 3 of 67 home parenteral-nutrition patients required hospitalisation and 2 had MRI-confirmed Wernicke encephalopathy (both resolved on high-dose IV thiamine). This has happened before, fatally: nationwide shortages in 1989 and 1996–97 each produced deaths from thiamine deficiency confirmed at autopsy. Verify that the multivitamin is actually in the bag. Check current status at ashp.org/drug-shortages and the FDA shortage database.
USPSTF alcohol screening update in progressAug 2025 draftThe draft retains Grade B for adults ≥18 including pregnancy, and Grade I for adolescents 12–17. A published final version could not be confirmed as of July 2026 — cite the 2018 statement and note the pending update.
GLP-1 receptor agonists — both a cause and a possible treatment2025–26ASMBS now recommends starting thiamine ≥2 weeks before medical weight-loss therapy because of Wernicke cases from rapid GLP-1-associated weight loss. Simultaneously, a 2026 randomised trial found semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly reduced heavy-drinking days more than placebo (treatment difference −13.7 percentage points, p = 0.0015). No guideline recommends GLP-1 agonists for alcohol use disorder — investigational only.
No EFNS/EAN update; no new biomarkeras of Jul 2026EFNS 2010 remains the only neurology-society guideline. Whole-blood thiamine by HPLC, with its 3–6 day turnaround, remains the only assay — there is no point-of-care test and no validated CSF or serum biomarker.

How to use this page safely. This is an educational reference built for internal medicine residents, not a substitute for clinical judgement, your institution's protocols, or a pharmacist. Doses are cited to their sources above; verify them against your local formulary before prescribing. Where the evidence is genuinely uncertain — the magnesium target, the loop-diuretic association, the optimal thiamine dose — this guide says so rather than inventing a number.
